title: Finite-Size Graph-RH for the GeoVac Hopf Graphs: Ihara Zeta, Bound-Crossing, and a Scope Boundary on Selberg-on-Hydrogen
abstract: We compute the Ihara zeta function of the two GeoVac Hopf graphs – the Fock-projected $S^3$ graph for the Coulomb problem [ref] and the Bargmann–Segal $S^5$ graph for the 3D isotropic harmonic oscillator [ref] – via the Ihara–Bass determinantal formula [ref] and the Hashimoto non-backtracking edge operator [ref]. Four results emerge. (1) Graph-Ramanujan at small sizes, bound-crossing at modest sizes: every graph tested at small sizes ($S^3$ at $n_{\max}=2,3$; $S^5$ at $N_{\max}=2,3$) satisfies the Kotani–Sunada [ref] graph-RH (Ramanujan) bound strictly, with deviations of the largest non-trivial Hashimoto eigenvalue from $\sqrt{q_{\max}}$ ranging from $-0.198$ ($S^3$, $n_{\max}=3$) to $-0.357$ ($S^5$, $N_{\max}=3$). A follow-on post-draft extension to $n_{\max},N_{\max}\in\{4,5\}$ finds that two of four graph families cross the bound at modest sizes (scalar $S^5$ at $N_{\max}=5$, Dirac-$S^3$ Rule B at $n_{\max}=4$) through real non-trivial eigenvalues, the non-real spectrum staying inside $\sqrt{q_{\max}}$ as Kotani–Sunada's theorem requires, while the scalar $S^3$ graph, whose $\ell$-blocks are disconnected components, stays below the bound on every component through $n_{\max}=5$; the graph-RH for GeoVac is therefore a finite-size statement for the families that cross. (2) Algebraicity of zeros: every $ζ_G(s)^{-1}$ factors as a product of integer-coefficient polynomials; no transcendental ($π$, $ζ(2)$, $ζ(3)$) enters the zero set. This sharpens Paper 24's $π$-free certificate [ref] from the adjacency data to the Ihara zeta. (3) Structural factorization, validated: the $S^3$ Coulomb zeta decomposes per $\ell$-shell because the Fock adjacency preserves $\ell$; the $S^5$ $N_{\max}=3$ zeta factors as $(s\pm 1)^{23}\cdot P_{12}(s^2)\cdot P_{22}(s^2)$, and the $12+22$ dichotomy is exactly the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ $m_\ell\to-m_\ell$ block decomposition of the node-level Ihara–Bass matrix — the only sub-action of the azimuthal $U(1)$ of the magnetic labels that commutes with a real integer adjacency. The analogous $22+24$ decomposition holds for the Dirac-$S^3$ Rule B $n_{\max}=3$ graph under $m_j\to-m_j$; this magnetic reflection is a fixed-point-free (Kramers) graph automorphism, whereas its chirality companion $\chi\to-\chi$ is not a graph symmetry at all — the two spinor-bundle chiralities differing in size by the discrete Dirac index $n_{\max}(n_{\max}+1)$, which explains the failure of relativistic $\mathbb{Z}_2$ tapering. (4) Scope boundary: Fock's Wick rotation $S^3\to H^3$ is mathematically clean [ref] but produces no natural discrete quotient $H^3/\Gamma$ from framework invariants; the Selberg-zeta direction on hyperbolic quotients of hydrogen is therefore structurally closed. The Ihara-to-classical-$ζ$ bridge is additionally blocked by bipartiteness (odd-argument Dirichlet characters such as $\chi_{-4}$ have support disjoint from the Ihara walk-length spectrum), and the direct bridge from the spectral-side Dirichlet series of Paper 28 to classical RH is closed as well.

title: The GeoVac Spectral Triple: A Synthesis Paper Locking the Framework into the Marcolli–van Suijlekom Gauge-Network Lineage
abstract: The GeoVac framework has, over Papers 0–31, accumulated a body of structural results—the $S^3$ Fock-projection equivalence (Paper 7 [ref]), the angular sparsity theorem (Paper 22 [ref]), the periods of Dirac spectral sums on $S^3$ (Paper 28 [ref]), the Bargmann–Segal $S^5$ HO lattice (Paper 24 [ref]), Wilson lattice gauge theory on the label graphs (Paper 30 [ref]), and the universal/Coulomb partition (Paper 31 [ref])—each self-contained but together suggesting one parent structure. [INTERNAL THEOREM] This paper names and constructs that structure: a finite spectral triple $(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{GV}}, \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{GV}}, D_{\mathrm{GV}})$ on the Fock-projected $S^3$ graph, with $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{GV}}$ the algebra of complex functions on graph nodes, $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{GV}}$ the Camporesi–Higuchi spinor space restricted to the truncation, and $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$ the diagonal Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac operator [ref] on the truncated spinor space of unit $S^3$ (no graph form is attached to $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$; Remark (ref)). This is not a new derivation; it is a structural map. Three results follow. [OBSERVATION] (1) Lineage. The construction sits inside the published Marcolli–van Suijlekom gauge-network framework [ref] (with the Perez-Sanchez correction [ref] that the continuum limit is Yang–Mills without Higgs), and inside the Connes–van Suijlekom spectral-truncation program [ref]. Every structural ingredient of the GeoVac construction has published precedent; what is not duplicated is \gvc{k-combination-rule}{the $α$ observation ($K = π(B + F - \Delta)$ matches $α^{-1}$ to $4.8 × 10^{-7}$;\ the root of the cubic $1/α = K - α^2$ matches to $8.8 × 10^{-8}$; Paper 2 [ref])} from a discrete spectral construction. [OBSERVATION] (2) Sub-sector identification. Paper 28's Dirac spectral sums on $S^3$ are sums over the spectrum of $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$, and the spectral action on that spectrum is Paper 51's [ref]; Paper 31's universal/Coulomb partition is the $\mathcal{A}/D$ split of the present triple's spectral data. Paper 30's compact $U(1)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ Wilson actions are read as the Cartan-torus and full non-abelian slices of an almost-commutative extension by $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, but through the gauge-network (edge-hopping) Dirac of those papers, not through $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$: the diagonal $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$ commutes with every $π(f)$ and so admits no inner fluctuations. These are read as four projections of one structure, at the level of spectral and algebraic data. [INTERNAL THEOREM] (3) Axiom audit. $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{GV}}$ is finite, involutive, faithfully represented on $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{GV}}$; $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$ is self-adjoint, and since $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$ and every $π(a)$ are diagonal in the same basis, $[D_{\mathrm{GV}}, π(a)] = 0$ identically: the diagonal triple is a spectral, not a metric, object (the metric role belongs to the non-diagonal multipliers of the truncated operator system on the true Camporesi–Higuchi window — the span of complete Dirac eigenspaces, Paper 38 [ref] — whose state spaces are proved to converge under the left-translation Lipschitz seminorm; convergence in the Dirac-commutator seminorm is [OPEN], that seminorm being non-degenerate on the window only as measured at $n_{\max} \le 3$). A real structure $J_{\mathrm{GV}}$ exists on the Dirac sector with $J_{\mathrm{GV}}^2 = -\mathbb{1}$ (the quaternionic/pseudoreal sign for the 2-dimensional Dirac spinor representation of $\mathrm{Spin}(3) = \mathrm{SU}(2)$) and $J_{\mathrm{GV}} D_{\mathrm{GV}} = +D_{\mathrm{GV}} J_{\mathrm{GV}}$, the signs $(\epsilon, \epsilon') = (-1, +1)$ of the continuum $S^3$ factor ($\mathrm{KO}$-dimension $3$ mod $8$ [ref]). The continuum factor is odd, and so is the true Camporesi–Higuchi window (measured, $n_{\max} \le 3$: the commutant of its operator system is the scalars), the truncation that converges; only the chirality-doubled Fock/Weyl model truncation is even, via the chirality-doubling grading $\gamma_{\mathrm{GV}} = \sigma_x ⊗ \mathbb{1}$, with sign triple $(-,+,+)$ and no $\mathrm{KO}$ label attached at finite cutoff. [MEASURED] On the Fock/Weyl model of the operator system (the computational object of this paper, in its Weyl and chirality-doubled forms) the order-zero and order-one conditions fail at finite $n_{\max}$, with residuals that grow over the measured cutoffs (order zero at $n_{\max} = 2, 3, 4$, order one at $n_{\max} = 2, 3$; mechanism open). [MEASURED] On the true Camporesi–Higuchi window that converges, the charge conjugation $J\psi = (i\sigma_y)\overline{\psi}$ satisfies $J^2 = -\mathbb{1}$, $JD = +DJ$ and $J\mathcal{O}J^{-1} = \mathcal{O}$ exactly, while order zero and order one fail from $n_{\max} = 1$ with residuals that grow toward the sup-norm scale of the generators; there every residual is a Toeplitz boundary term of the compression, confined to the top Dirac levels of the window. [OBSERVATION] The four-way $S^3$ coincidence—Fock projection image, Hopf bundle total space $S³$ (base $S^2$), Camporesi–Higuchi spin carrier, $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ gauge manifold—is the statement that the manifold reached by the operator-system truncations in the continuum limit, the spinor bundle of the Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac, and the gauge group of the $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ almost-commutative extension (Paper 30) all coincide on the unique rank-1 non-abelian compact simply-connected Lie group. \noindentScope. This paper does not derive new physics. It synthesizes existing GeoVac results into the axiomatic spectral-triple language. The synthesis lifts each result from a free-standing observation to a sub-sector of a single named structure, and makes explicit which axioms hold rigorously, which hold up to the standard finite-truncation caveats, and which remain open. [PANEL-VERIFIED] The real-structure question—whether the GeoVac Dirac operator $D_{\mathrm{GV}}$ (the diagonal spectral form) carries a real structure matching the signs of $S^3$ exactly at finite $n_{\max}$ or only in the continuum limit—is resolved in favour of finite-$n_{\max}$ exactness for the three $J$-relations $J^2 = -\mathbb{1}$, $JD = +DJ$, $J\mathcal{O}J^{-1} = \mathcal{O}$ only, measured on the Fock/Weyl model objects and, independently, on the true Camporesi–Higuchi window. [MEASURED] The order-zero and order-one conditions fail at finite $n_{\max}$ with residuals that grow with the cutoff, on the Fock/Weyl model of the operator system and on the true window alike (on the true window as a boundary term of the compression). The Fock/Weyl model truncation is even (chirality doubling; sign triple $(-,+,+)$, no $\mathrm{KO}$ label); the true window is odd (measured, $n_{\max} \le 3$), like the continuum (its operator system generates all of $B(\mathcal{H})$, so it admits no grading), and there the pair $(\varepsilon, \varepsilon') = (-,+)$ is forced by equivariance; the residual open items are catalogued in Sec. (ref).

title: State-space Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of truncated Camporesi–Higuchi spectral triples on S³
abstract: [INTERNAL THEOREM] We prove, unconditionally, that the Connes–van Suijlekom truncations of the round $S³ = SU(2)$ Camporesi–Higuchi spectral triple converge to the continuum spectral triple in van Suijlekom's state-space Gromov–Hausdorff distance [ref]: the bound $d_{\mathrm{GH}} \le \gamma_{n_max}$, with $\gamma_{n_max}$ the mass-concentration moment of the central spectral Fejér kernel on $SU(2)$, and $\gamma_{n_max} \to 0$ are proved. For that kernel \( \gamma_{n_max} = (4/π + o(1)) \log n_max / n_max \) (dual-Coxeter normalisation of the $SU(2)$ metric; $2/π$ on the unit round $S³$) is [INTERNAL THEOREM + MEASURED] (Appendix (ref)). The proof uses the Fejér amplitude only as a real central amplitude in the spinor window, so any such amplitude gives the same bound with its own moment; [MEASURED] a Ces\`aro-tapered amplitude gives $d_{\mathrm{GH}} = O(1/n_max)$. The constant $4/π$ therefore belongs to the Fejér kernel, not to the convergence rate; a proof of the $O(1/n_max)$ rate and its optimal constant are [OPEN]. [INTERNAL THEOREM] The truncated state spaces are metrized by the left-translation Lipschitz seminorm, which equals the Dirac/metric Lipschitz constant on the continuum and whose kernel at every finite cutoff is exactly the scalars. ([MEASURED] On the true Camporesi–Higuchi window the Dirac-commutator seminorm also has kernel exactly the scalars at $n_max \le 3$, by two independent constructions (the second at $n_max \le 2$); on a doubled Fock model it does not, Remark (ref). Whether the convergence can be proved directly in the Dirac seminorm is [OPEN]; the proof uses the translation seminorm because its compression estimates close.) The proof is a compression/lifted-state argument in the pattern of the compact-metric-group theorem of Gaudillot-Estrada–van Suijlekom [ref], with self-contained proofs: the dual map evaluates conjugated operators against the central spectral Fejér vector state, which embeds exactly into the spinor window via the $\mathrm{SU}(2)_L × \mathrm{SU}(2)_R$ block decomposition $V_j ⊗ (V_{j \pm 1/2})$ of the Camporesi–Higuchi eigenspaces (the truncated Hilbert space is the span of complete eigenspaces; \S(ref)), and both almost-inverse defects collapse to Fejér smoothing — one on functions, one as operator conjugation-averaging — at the common moment $\gamma_{n_max}$. The contribution relative to the scalar theory: the spinor-window transport, per-band injectivity of the compression on the Camporesi–Higuchi window (bands $N \le 2n_max$), and the closed-form Fejér moment. Supporting structure is organized in four lemmas: (L1$'$) [PANEL-VERIFIED] a finite-distance statement on a doubled computational model of the truncated operator system (not used by the theorem; \S(ref)); (L2) [INTERNAL THEOREM + MEASURED] \gvc{p38-rate-constant}{a positive central spectral Fejér kernel on $SU(2)$ with closed-form mass-concentration moment and Stein–Weiss-type asymptotics $\gamma_n \sim (4/π)\log n / n$ (dual-Coxeter normalisation; $2/π$ on the unit $S³$)}; (L3) [INTERNAL THEOREM] a Lipschitz comparison bound $\opnorm{[\DCH, \Mat_f]} \leq C_3 \norm{\nabla f}_{L^\infty}$ with $C_3 = 1$, by compression from the continuum identity (not used by the unconditional theorem); (L4) [INTERNAL THEOREM] a Berezin map (convolution form) that is positive, contractive, an approximate identity, and L3-compatible. [OBSERVATION] The Fejér constant equals (numerically) a quotient of sphere volumes — $2/π = \Vol(S^2)/\Vol(S³)$ at unit radius, and twice that, $4/π$, in the dual-Coxeter normalisation of \S(ref) — and not the Hopf fibration's base-to-total ratio (\S(ref)). The $\logn_max$ factor is the first-moment logarithm of the Fejér-type (squared-Dirichlet; on the circle, the Ces\`aro-1 Fejér) kernel, which the circle's Fejér kernel already carries (Remark (ref)); it is a property of the kernel, not of the convergence, and a tapered amplitude removes it [MEASURED]. State-space Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of scalar truncations for compact metric groups with bi-invariant metric — including $SU(2)$ — is established by Gaudillot-Estrada–van Suijlekom [ref];\ the residual contribution here is the Camporesi–Higuchi spinor substrate and the closed-form Fejér moment. The construction supplies quantitative convergence data toward the continuum target $S³$, the commutative factor that almost-commutative spectral-triple constructions hosted on $S³$ [ref] take as input;\ convergence of an almost-commutative structure itself is not treated here and is [OPEN].

title: State-space Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of truncated tensor-product Camporesi–Higuchi spectral triples on S³ × S³
State-space Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of spectral truncations of compact semisimple Lie groups with bi-invariant metric
abstract: Let $G$ be a compact connected semisimple Lie group of rank $r \ge 1$ equipped with a bi-invariant Riemannian metric, and let $\Tcal_G = (C^\infty(G), L^2(G, \Sigma), \Dop_G)$ denote its canonical metric spectral triple, with $\Dop_G$ the Kostant cubic Dirac operator. For each cutoff $\Lammax > 0$, let $\Tcal_\Lammax = (\Op_\Lammax, \Hilb_\Lammax, P_\Lammax \Dop_G P_\Lammax)$ denote the Connes–van Suijlekom spectral truncation obtained by projection onto irreducibles with Casimir $\le \Lammax^2$. We prove that (for $SU(2)$; for general $G$ conditionally on the per-group spin-window decomposition, see below) $\Tcal_\Lammax$ converges to $\Tcal_G$ in van Suijlekom's state-space Gromov–Hausdorff distance, with the state spaces metrized by the left-translation Lipschitz seminorm as in Paper 38 (convergence in the Dirac-commutator seminorm is open), with $$ d_{\mathrm{GH}}(\Tcal_\Lammax, \Tcal_G) \;\le\; \gamma_\Lammax(G) \;\to\; 0, \qquad \gamma_\Lammax(SU(2)) = \frac{2}{π} \frac{\log \Lammax}{\Lammax} + O(1/\Lammax), $$ with constant $1$ from the lifted-state route of Paper 38 (the Lipschitz comparison constant $C_3(G) = 1$ of Lemma (ref) enters only the withdrawn approximation-pair route). The $SU(2)$ moment constant $2/π$ [INTERNAL THEOREM] is Paper 38's $(4/π)\log n/n$ read in the cutoff variable used here: $\mathrm{Cas}(\mathrm{ad}) = h^\vee = 2$ on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ fixes $\langle X, Y\rangle = -2 \mathrm{tr}(XY)$, whose geodesic distance from the identity is the rotation angle — exactly the distance Paper 38 integrates against — and Paper 38's shell index is $n_{\max} = 2j_{\max} + 1$, so $n \simeq 2\Lammax$. It is a kernel constant, not the convergence rate: a tapered amplitude gives $O(1/\Lammax)$ on $SU(2)$ [MEASURED], Paper 38; for general $G$ this is open. Because $\gamma_\Lammax \Lammax$ is invariant under rescaling the bi-invariant metric, the constant in $\Lammax$ does not depend on the normalisation; Paper 38's values $4/π$ (dual-Coxeter) and $2/π$ (unit $S^3$) are per its shell index $n$. Whether the leading constant $c(G)$ of $\gamma_\Lammax(G)$ is the same for every compact connected simple $G$ is [OPEN]. Paper 38 [ref] is recovered as the rank-$1$ case $G = SU(2)$. The proof is the lifted-state route (UCP compression plus the conjugation average against the L2 central spectral Fejér kernel with closed-form quantitative rate); the lemma chain (L1$'$ operator system, L3 Lipschitz comparison with constant $1$ at every rank, proved by compression, L4 Berezin reconstruction via Peter–Weyl) supplies the substrate and supporting estimates, L3 entering only the withdrawn approximation-pair route. The approximation pair of \S(ref) is recorded but does not supply an independent proof: its dual reach is a named gap and both height constituents are refuted (Lemma (ref), corrected 2026-09-04). [OBSERVATION] Paper 38 reads its Fejér-moment constant (a reading, not a derivation) as the $k=0$ volume-slot content of a master Mellin engine $\mathcal M[\Tr(D^k e^{-tD^2})]$ on the spectral triple; whether the value so read extends from $SU(2)$ to the other simple groups is open with $c(G)$: a Plancherel $×$ Vandermonde cancellation is proposed as the mechanism (a proof sketch), and the rank-$2$ and rank-$3$ extractions reported here compare mismatched conventions and do not test it (status note in \S(ref)). For $SU(2)$ the result supplies an explicit rate (translation-seminorm metrization) for the state-space Gromov–Hausdorff convergence proved by Gaudillot-Estrada and van Suijlekom [ref]; for general $G$ it gives the bound $d_{\mathrm{GH}} \le \gamma_\Lammax(G) \to 0$, conditionally, with the rate form open. The strictly stronger Latrémolière propinquity is not claimed: its dual-reach step is a named gap (Remark (ref)), exactly as for the rank-1 case (Paper 38). Moreover the general-$G$ lifted-state construction underlying even the state-space GH statement is verified only for $SU(2)$, so for general $G$ the convergence is conditional on that per-group spin-window decomposition; the closed-form moment $\gamma_\Lammax(G)$ (the genuine new content) is unaffected. For semisimple $G$ with more than one simple factor the leading constant is open (Remark (ref)).

title: Tomita–Takesaki modular structure on truncated SU(2) spectral triples: the four-witness 2π period at finite cutoff
abstract: The four-witness Wick-rotation theorem (Hartle–Hawking [ref], Sewell [ref], Bisognano–Wichmann [ref], Unruh [ref]) asserts that a state of a quantum field restricted to a region bounded by a bifurcate Killing horizon with surface gravity $\kappa_g$ is KMS at inverse temperature $\beta = 2π/\kappa_g$ with respect to Killing-time evolution. The shared $2π$ across all four faces is $\Vol(S^1)$, the regularity period of the Euclidean rotation of the observer's causal-domain coordinates. That continuum statement is prior art and is not re-proved here. We study its finite-cutoff period on the Connes–van Suijlekom [ref] truncated Camporesi–Higuchi [ref] spectral triple $\Tcal_{n_max}$, with a hemispheric wedge and a posited wedge generator $K_α^W = \mathrm{diag}(2m_j)$ on the $m_j > 0$ wedge states, a relabelling built from the doubled polar rotation generator $2J_z$ (whose own compression to the wedge is zero). Because $K_α^W$ has integer spectrum, $e^{2π i K_α^W} = I$, and the conjugation flow closes, $\sigma_{2π}(O) = O$, for every operator $O$ — an elementary fact [SYMBOLIC] that holds for any integer-spectrum generator whatsoever and therefore does not single out a Bisognano–Wichmann modular flow. The Tomita–Takesaki reading is not an independent check: the wedge state is defined as $\rho_W = e^{-K_α^W}/Z$, so Tomita's theorem for a Gibbs state returns the same generator, $\sigma_t^{\TT} = \sigma_{-t}^{α}$. Nor is the agreement of the four witnesses (Bisognano–Wichmann, Hartle–Hawking, Sewell, Unruh) a finite-cutoff result: the six witness instantiations use the same $K_α^W$ with the surface gravity $\kappa_g$ relabelled, and $\beta H_{\mathrm{local}} = K_α^W$ is $\kappa_g$-independent by construction, so their bit-identical residuals hold by construction. We record these closures (bit-exact in floating point at $n_max \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}$, residual $O(\sqrt{\dim \Hilb_{n_max}} \cdot \varepsilon_{\mathrm{machine}})$) as what they are. We also record the operator-level distinction between $2J_z$ ($e^{2π i K} = +I$) and the wedge-restricted Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac (half-integer spectrum, $e^{2π i D_W} = -I$, the spinor double-cover sign; the conjugation flow closes for both). The genuine finite-cutoff question — derive $K$ as the modular Hamiltonian of a wedge-restricted Camporesi–Higuchi state, rather than posit it — is [OPEN]. The Lorentzian extension to signature $(3, 1)$ via Bizi–Brouder–Besnard 2018 [ref] Krein-space spectral triples is carried out at finite cutoff in the present paper (\S(ref), which absorbs the former Paper 43): a Krein carrier and Krein-self-adjoint Lorentzian Dirac, an axiom audit at Bizi–Brouder–Besnard signature $(4, 6)$ in which the universal chirality anticommutation fails on the truthful Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac, the same automatic (and signature-blind) period closure, and a Hilbert–Schmidt orthogonality between the posited local Hamiltonian and the wedge Dirac that is a chirality-parity identity [SYMBOLIC], the only transcendental of its residual, $1/π^2$, being the posited $\beta = 2π/\kappa_g$ squared. Its continuum (Lorentzian-propinquity-rate) closure was described here as the named open frontier when this paper was drafted; that is superseded (2026-06, Paper 45 [ref]): the natural device fails structurally, and the chase is closed on the convention branch (an [ARGUED] reading: its Euclidean-only leg is generator-independent, its Wick-rotation/KMS-circle leg is conditional on O0 for the Bisognano–Wichmann generator; Paper 45 Q1). The mechanism is visible in this paper's own result (i): the posited wedge generator has integer spectrum, so the finite-cutoff flow is a compact $\beta = 2π$ circle rather than a non-compact boost [SYMBOLIC], and on the argued reading [ARGUED] every Lipschitz/boost seminorm built on it is signature-blind. The finite-cutoff closures reported below stand as computed; what does not follow from them is a metric statement about signature, or an identification of the posited generator with a Bisognano–Wichmann boost. The construction is a finite-dimensional illustration of the Connes–Rovelli thermal-time setup [ref] on a hemispheric wedge of the round $S³$, not a derivation of it.

title: Operator-system extension of the BBB Krein spectral triple at finite cutoff: propagation number and envelope dependence on the Camporesi–Higuchi spinor bundle
abstract: The Connes–van Suijlekom [ref] spectral truncation of $C^\infty(S³)$ on the round $S³ = SU(2)$ at cutoff $n_max$ produces a $*$-closed but not multiplicatively closed linear subspace $\Op_{n_max} \subset \Mat_{N}(\C)$ with propagation number $\prop(\Op_{n_max}) = 2$ (Paper 32 \S III, matching the Connes–vS worked example on the Toeplitz operator system $C(S^1)^{(n)}$ verbatim). We construct the natural Lorentzian extension $\Op_{n_max, \Nt}^L \subset \Bcal(\Krein_{n_max, \Nt})$ on the Bizi–Brouder–Besnard [ref] Krein spectral triple at signature $(s, t) = (3, 1)$, $(m, n) = (4, 6)$, in the Peskin–Schroeder chiral basis with Lorentzian Dirac $\DL = i\bigl(\gamma^0 ⊗ \partial_t + \DGV ⊗ I_{\Nt}\bigr)$ per van den Dungen 2016 [ref] Proposition 4.1, and the Camporesi–Higuchi [ref] spatial spinor bundle. Multipliers are tensor products of chirality-doubled spatial scalar $3$-$Y$ multipliers with a polynomial-basis temporal subalgebra on a finite uniform $t$-grid. At $\Nt = 1$ the construction reduces bit-identically to the Riemannian chirality-doubled operator system on the FullDirac Hilbert space, with Frobenius residual exactly $0.0$ in float64. We prove $\Op_{n_max, \Nt}^L$ is a Lorentzian truncated operator system (it is $*$-closed, contains the identity, and is not multiplicatively closed) and exhibit a witness pair lifting the Paper 32 \S III witness verbatim. The principal structural finding is that the propagation number is envelope-dependent: targeting the natural Weyl-doubled achievable envelope $\dim_\Weyl^2 \cdot \Nt$, we measure $\prop(\Op_{n_max, \Nt}^L) = 2$ at $n_max \in \{2, 3\}$ [MEASURED], the value Paper 32 \S III finds on the scalar Fock system; targeting the full $\Bcal(\Krein)$ envelope $\dim_\Krein^2$, we obtain $\prop = \infty$ at every cell. The Weyl-doubling and the commutative temporal subalgebra block scalar multipliers from generating chirality-flipping or non-diagonal temporal operators; the achievable envelope is the correct natural target for scalar-multiplier closure on the spinor bundle. A separate substantive finding is that the Krein-positive restriction is trivial: every chirality-doubled scalar multiplier $M \oplus M$ commutes with the chirality-swap fundamental symmetry $\JL$, so $\Op^{L,+} = \Op^L$ exactly. The natural Krein-positive seminorm device is annihilated (Paper 45), so any remaining route has to carry the signature somewhere other than the seminorm (the former Sprint L3b propinquity route is descoped with Paper 45, 2026-06-09; see \S (ref)). Honest scope: this paper closes the operator-system substrate at finite cutoff; Lorentzian-propinquity convergence is descoped (Paper 45). No published Lorentzian propinquity construction exists as of May 2026:\ Latrémolière 2017/2023 [ref] and Leimbach–van Suijlekom 2024 [ref] are strictly Riemannian.

title: Lorentzian propinquity on truncated SU(2)×U(1)_T Krein spectral triples: a degeneracy theorem
abstract: We construct truncated Krein spectral triples over the compact-temporal Wick-rotated manifold $\Manifold = S³ × \SoneT$:\ $\Krein_{n_max,\Nt} := \HGV^{n_max} ⊗ \C^{\Nt}$ is the chirality-doubled Camporesi–Higuchi spinor space tensored with the $\Nt$-mode Fourier truncation of $L^{2}(\SoneT)$, with fundamental symmetry $\JL = \JL^{\spat} ⊗ I_{\Nt}$ at the Bizi–Brouder–Besnard [ref] classification $(m, n) = (4, 6)$, Lorentzian Dirac $\DL = i(\gamma^{0} ⊗ \partial_{t} + \DGV ⊗ I_{\Nt})$ per van den Dungen 2016 [ref] Proposition 4.1, and operator system built from chirality-doubled scalar $3$-$Y$ spatial multipliers tensored with momentum-diagonal temporal multipliers. The natural device for a ``Lorentzian propinquity'' on this family is to compress to the Krein-positive subspace $\Kplus$, where the Krein product is a positive-definite Hilbert inner product, and to apply Riemannian quantum-metric machinery to the compressed triple $(\Pplus\Op^{L}\Pplus, \Kplus, \Pplus\DL\Pplus)$. Our main theorem shows that this device fails structurally (Theorem (ref)): Krein-self-adjointness of the anti-Hermitian spatial block forces $\{\JL, \DGV ⊗ I_{\Nt}\} = 0$, so the compression annihilates the spatial Dirac, $\Pplus(\DGV ⊗ I)\Pplus = 0$, while the momentum-diagonal temporal multipliers commute with the surviving temporal block; the compressed-Dirac Lipschitz seminorm therefore vanishes identically on the operator system built from spatial and momentum-diagonal multipliers (verified bit-exactly at $(n_max, \Nt) \in \{(2,3), (3,5)\}$: kernel $= 100%$ of that multiplier basis), and no quantum Gromov–Hausdorff-type distance is defined on it. The annihilation is thus multiplier-algebra specific, not absolute: the Toeplitz temporal multipliers named below as the open target survive the same compression ($s_{\Kplus}(I_s ⊗ S_q) = \omega_q$ exactly; Status note 2026-06-18) — nonzero but still degenerate, since the spatial multipliers stay in its kernel — and the surviving seminorm carries no indefinite-signature content even under a genuine temporal Krein involution — a sharpened ``weakens-to-convention'' verdict. What does hold: the operator-level $\JL$-equivariance of the Berezin/truncation pair; the structural identity $[\DL, a_{s} ⊗ a_{t}] = i[\DGV, a_{s}] ⊗ a_{t}$, which is precisely the diagnosis that the momentum-diagonal temporal algebra is metrically invisible; and a spatial convergence statement (Proposition (ref)): the spatial truncations converge in van Suijlekom's state-space Gromov–Hausdorff distance [ref] at the companion-paper rate $O(\logn_max/n_max)$ — unconditional, via the companion paper's translation-seminorm theorem — with the temporal factor a metrically invisible spectator carried $\JL$-equivariantly. The genuine Lorentzian/Krein quantum-metric convergence problem — a temporal multiplier algebra the Dirac can see (Toeplitz compressions of $e^{iqt}$) and a Krein-compatible Lipschitz seminorm that does not compress $\DL$ — is stated as an open target with a sharpened specification (\S (ref)). An earlier draft of this paper claimed a convergence theorem through the compression device; that claim is retracted (Remark (ref)).

title: Boundary CFT_3-on-S³ observables and the GeoVac spectral triple: partition function and wedge KMS entropy
abstract: We exhibit three complementary boundary-side quantities, framed by standard CFT$_{3}$-on-$S³$ calculations, around the GeoVac spectral triple, each obtained by a structurally distinct operation — (A) from the full, untruncated continuum spectra of the conformally coupled scalar and Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac operators on the round $S³$, (B) from the wedge KMS state $\rhoW = e^{-\Kalpha}/Z$ built on the truncated triple from a posited wedge generator, (C) by comparing that generator with a continuum one: (A) the universal F-theorem coefficient $F_{S³}$, the standard zeta-regularised determinant $-\tfrac{1}{2}ζ'_{\Delta}(0)$ of the continuum spectrum, is re-derived in closed Hurwitz form and agrees with the Klebanov–Pufu–Safdi (2011) values (symbolically for the Dirac, to 61 digits with PSLQ identification for the scalar) for both the conformally coupled scalar ($F_{s} = \tfrac{\log 2}{8} - \tfrac{3ζ(3)}{16π^{2}}$) and the free Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac ($F_{D} = \tfrac{\log 2}{4} + \tfrac{3ζ(3)}{8π^{2}}$) — an independent re-derivation of known continuum values, in which the finite cutoff $n_max$ never enters; (B) the wedge KMS entropy on the truncated triple has the exact asymptotic $S(\rhoW) = 2\logn_max + (\coth 1 - \log(2\sinh 1)) + O(1/n_max)$, whose slope $2$ is the exponent of the $\simn_max^{2}$ degeneracy of the lowest shell of the posited generator $\Kalpha$ (the slope is independent of the inverse temperature; the constant is the unit-$\beta$ value, and $\rhoW$ is not the Bisognano–Wichmann-normalised state, which would be $e^{-π\Kalpha}/Z$ since $\Kalpha$ carries the values of $2J_{z}$; the $2$ is not the dimension of the entangling surface, which for a CFT$_{3}$ is a circle); (C) the framework's wedge generator $\Kalpha$ (a posited relabelling built from the polar rotation generator $J_{\mathrm{polar}} = 2J_z$, not derived from a state) shares a discrete integer spectrum and closure at rotation angle $2π$ (its adjoint flow closes at $t = π$) with the Euclidean rotation generator whose Wick rotation is the continuum Casini–Huerta–Myers modular Hamiltonian of a hemispherical cap of the spatial $S^{2}$ (the latter itself generates a boost-like flow with continuous spectrum); this is a structural analogy with the Euclidean generator only, and the identification of $\Kalpha$ as the modular Hamiltonian of a wedge-restricted state is [OPEN] (2026-09-28; see [ref]). The scalar/Dirac free energies decompose orthogonally into their two transcendental sectors: $F_{D} + 2 F_{s} = \log(2)/2$ isolates the $\log 2$ sector (a level-2 cyclotomic period, in the ring of the M3 sub-mechanism of the master Mellin engine of [ref]), and $F_{D} - 2 F_{s} = 3ζ(3)/(4π^{2})$ isolates the $ζ(3)/π^{2}$ sector (an M1$×$M3 cross-product), following the engine's period-ring stratification [ref]; no Seeley–DeWitt (M2) content appears in these values. This is a decomposition of the continuum KPS values, and the first application of the master Mellin engine's tagging to independently published (non-GeoVac-internal) values. The F-theorem values themselves are due to [ref] and are not new; the present paper's contributions are (i) their independent re-derivation from the continuum spectra via closed Hurwitz forms (with PSLQ confirmation), (ii) the orthogonal $\log 2$ / $ζ(3)/π^{2}$ dual-basis decomposition of those continuum values, classified as M3-ring and M1$×$M3 content (Theorem (ref)), and (iii) the exact large-$n_max$ asymptotic of the wedge-KMS entropy on the truncated triple, a lowest-shell degeneracy count. The framework has no bulk, so none of this is holographic. The CHM comparison (C) is recorded as an analogy only: $\Kalpha$ is posited, and a GH distance between spectral triples does not bound the convergence of one operator to another. The bulk-side identifications (Ryu–Takayanagi minimum surfaces, JLMS bulk-modular reconstruction, AdS$_{4}$ / H$^{4}$ dual geometry) are blocked at the framework's existing infrastructure: zero AdS / H$^{4}$ machinery, and the Wick-rotation $S³ \to H^{3}$ supplies no natural discrete subgroup [ref].

title: Spectral truncation of the flat plane: state-space convergence with a squared window, and the disk-with-cone left open
abstract: The spectral-truncation convergence results of the companion Papers [ref] treat compact groups, where a Fejér-type kernel is available and the state spaces are compact. We treat the flat plane $ℝ^{2}$ — non-compact, but with a transitive translation group. Truncate $L^{2}(ℝ^{2})$ to the band-limited subspace $\Hilb_{\Lambda}$ (Fourier support $|\xi|\le\sqrt\Lambda$), compress bounded uniformly continuous multipliers into it, and metrize the truncated state space by the translation Lipschitz seminorm. With a lift built from the translates of one window vector $\psi_{\Lambda}\in\Hilb_{\Lambda}$, the compression/lifted-state argument of Paper 38 (whose scalar compact-group form is due to Gaudillot-Estrada and van Suijlekom [ref]) goes through with the positive kernel $|\psi_{\Lambda}|^{2}$. Four estimates hold with the single constant $\gamma_{\Lambda}=\int|x| |\psi_{\Lambda}(x)|^{2}dx= \gamma_{1}\Lambda^{-1/2}$ [INTERNAL THEOREM], and they give a Gromov–Hausdorff bound $d_{\mathrm{GH}}\le\gamma_{\Lambda}$ between the Monge–Kantorovich state spaces, taken over the states of finite first moment [INTERNAL THEOREM] for those state classes; whether they are the canonical ones is open. The window must have a finite first moment. The sharp ball window does not: its first moment diverges logarithmically. The smooth-edged windows $(1-|\xi|^{2})_{+}^{m}$ with $m\ge1$ do; for $m=1$, $\gamma_{1}=32/(5π)$. The two-dimensional Bochner–Riesz map is not a usable lift: its kernel is negative somewhere at every order, and its Lebesgue constant exceeds $1$ [PRIOR ART] (both classical facts [ref], with a one-line argument recorded here). On the finite Dirichlet disk-with-cone the paper reports measurements. The Markov–Ces\`aro reconstruction map is not positivity-preserving (a ring counterexample), and its reconstruction error on the open disk decays on every tested observable. Convergence on the disk, and on the cone with apex angle $α\ne1$ (which has no translation group), is left open.

title: The Molecular Fock Projection: Diatomic Molecules as Prolate Spheroidal Lattices
abstract: Fock's 1935 stereographic projection maps the hydrogen atom onto the unit three-sphere $S^3$, where the Schrödinger equation becomes a pure Laplace–Beltrami eigenvalue problem with no potential term. The GeoVac program builds a graph on the $S^3$ label set $(n,l,m)$, on which $-\Delta_{S^3}$ is the diagonal $SO(4)$ Casimir $n^2-1$ at every cutoff, from which the hydrogenic energies follow through Fock's energy shell $p_0^2 = -2E$ (Papers 0, 1, 7);\ the graph Laplacian itself is not a discretization of the $S^3$ operator and does not converge to it, and its extremal eigenvalue matches the hydrogen ground state only by construction through the scale $\kappa = -1/16$ (Paper 7). For molecules, however, $S^3$ is not the natural geometry: the single-$p_0$ momentum scale cannot encode the $R$-dependent bonding physics in that single-$n$ shared-$p_0$ approximation (Paper 8–9, negative theorem; the genuine cross-$n$ Coulomb–Sturmian basis escapes it, and a validated two-centre Coulomb–Sturmian H$_2$ CI binds, Paper 60). We resolve this by identifying the natural geometry principle: every separable quantum system has a natural lattice—the label set and channel structure of the coordinates in which separation occurs, within which the separated equations are then solved. For one-center systems that geometry is $S^3$ (where the GeoVac lattice is the label set, not a convergent discretization of the Laplace–Beltrami operator, Paper 7); for two-center systems it is the prolate spheroid. We discretize the separated prolate spheroidal equations for H$_2^+$ using a spectral angular solver (Legendre basis) and two radial solvers—a self-adjoint finite-difference (FD) scheme and a spectral Laguerre basis—with Brent root-finding in the separation parameter $c^2 = -R^2 E_{\mathrm{elec}}/2$ to enforce self-consistency. For $\sigma$ states ($m = 0$), the spectral Laguerre matrix elements can be computed algebraically from three-term recurrence relations, eliminating numerical quadrature entirely (the default path uses Gauss–Laguerre quadrature, which agrees to machine precision). For $π$ and $\delta$ states ($m \neq 0$), an associated Laguerre basis absorbs the centrifugal $1/x$ singularity via partial-fraction decomposition and Stieltjes integral recurrence, reducing the non-algebraic content to a single transcendental seed value $e^a E_1(a)$. The method has zero free parameters: all inputs are nuclear charges, internuclear distance, and basis/grid resolution. The separation constant is also an exact label. In any product (Laguerre $×$ Legendre) basis, the matrices of $H$ and of the Erikson–Hill operator $\Lambda$ are Atkinson operator determinants, so $[H,\Lambda]=0$ holds at every truncation (measured to $10^{-14}$). $\Lambda$ runs from $L^2$ in the united atom to the Runge–Lenz $A_z$ (parabolic) label in the separated atoms. [MEASURED, not regression-tested] For the Paper 12 H$_2$ CI at one basis and geometry it ranks configurations 8–10$×$ better than orbital energy, though natural orbitals beat it by about $10×$. It does not transfer to a LiH orbital set that is not tensor-closed. Results for H$_2^+$ with the spectral Laguerre radial solver ($n_{\mathrm{basis}} = 20$): total energy at $R = 2.0$ bohr $E = -0.602634214494936$ Ha, reproducing Peek's value $-0.6026342144949$ Ha at that distance [ref] to $3.6×10^{-14}$ Ha—below the last digit to which that reference is quoted, so the residual is reference-limited rather than a property of the method ([MEASURED]). Equilibrium bond length $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 1.9973$ bohr ($0.004%$ above the exact $1.99719$ bohr), and correct dissociation to H + p at $R \to \infty$. The spectral solver achieves a $250×$ dimension reduction and a $270×$ speedup over the FD solver, whose 1.01% error was a discretization artifact. This establishes the prolate spheroidal lattice as the molecular analog of Fock's atomic $S^3$ projection.

title: Algebraic Two-Electron Integrals on the Prolate Spheroidal Lattice
abstract: Paper 11 established the prolate spheroidal lattice as the natural geometry for diatomic molecules, solving H$_2^+$ to machine precision (spectral Laguerre solver) with zero free parameters. The extension to two electrons requires electron-electron repulsion integrals $\langle\phi_i|1/r_{12}|\phi_j\rangle$ over the six-dimensional two-particle configuration space. The standard approach—numerical quadrature on a grid in prolate spheroidal coordinates—converges slowly due to the Coulomb singularity at $r_{12} = 0$ and saturates at $\sim$80% of the exact H$_2$ dissociation energy $D_e$ as the basis grows. We replace numerical integration with algebraic evaluation using the Neumann expansion of $1/r_{12}$ in prolate spheroidal coordinates, which decomposes each six-dimensional integral into a finite sum of products of one-dimensional auxiliary integrals computable by recurrence relations. The resulting two-electron integrals are exact within the Neumann truncation order $L$, with no six-dimensional quadrature and no fitted parameters. The one step historically left to numerical integration—the log-singular second-kind Legendre moment $B_l$—also has a closed form (Sec. (ref)): the only transcendental content is the exponential integral $E_1$, the Euler–Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ and $\ln$, so in the $\sigma$ sector the reduction is fully quadrature-free. (The $|m| \ge 1$ channels keep the same kernel; generalising the same $A_l$, $B_l$, $X_l$ recurrences to associated Legendre functions (Sec. (ref)) gives a moment-recurrence engine that is stable in the $\delta$ ($|m| = 2$) sector where the differentiation route diverges, and—with the same closed-form seeds—is likewise fully quadrature-free.) A systematic convergence study on H$_2$ at $R = 1.4011$ bohr demonstrates that the Neumann algebraic $V_{ee}$ yields 92.2% of the exact $D_e$ with 27 basis functions, compared to 79.6% for numerical $V_{ee}$ at the same basis size—a uniform 12–20 percentage point improvement across all basis sizes from 1 to 72 functions. The Neumann result plateaus at 92.4%, confirming that $V_{ee}$ integration error has been eliminated. [MEASURED] The remaining 7.6% gap is a basis-space limit, and we identify which one. The basis used here is $\varphi$-independent, so it spans only $m_1 = m_2 = 0$ configurations; but a $^1\Sigma_g^+$ state constrains the total $M = m_1 + m_2$ to zero, not each $m_i$ separately, so the $π^2$, $\delta^2$, \ldots configurations—every one of them $^1\Sigma_g^+$—are absent by construction. Restoring them in the same basis with the same Neumann kernel gives $99.1%$ of $D_e$ at $|m| \le 1$ (stability envelope $99.0$–$99.1%$; Sec. (ref)), a gain of $11.6$ mHa that no growth along the $\sigma$ axis reproduces (near-tripling the $\sigma$ basis is worth $0.34$ mHa). [MEASURED] That $99.1%$ is where the monomial radial basis $\xi^j$ stalls—a Hankel moment problem whose overlap matrix is past double precision, not a structural ceiling. Re-basing the same span onto an orthogonal-polynomial family is an exact change of basis that removes the linear dependence, and the energy then climbs monotonically and variationally to $\gvq{p12_rebased_de_pct_aopt}{99.81}%$ of $D_e$ ($\gvq{p12_rebased_err_mha_aopt}{0.32}$ mHa, inside chemical accuracy) at a larger truncation and the variationally optimal exponent (Sec. (ref)). [MEASURED] An explicit-$r_{12}$ (James–Coolidge) extension of the algebraic engine, in which every $r_{12}$ matrix element reduces to the same $A K_0 - B K_1$ Neumann kernels as $V_{ee}$ (no quadrature), reaches $\gvq{p12_r12_err_mha}{0.053}$ mHa above the exact value—a sixfold reduction of the CI residual—confirming constructively that ordinary integer powers of $r_{12}$, not non-analytic terms, close the gap (Sec. (ref)). The same reduction—on one centre the classical Hylleraas-CI treatment of many-electron correlated integrals—extends without a resolution of identity to a heteronuclear diatomic (HeH$^+$) and through the complete many-body matrix elements of a two-center four-electron explicit-$r_{12}$ CI:\ the genuinely four-body Coulomb bridge and the two-center three-body triangle are both reduced RI-free—the latter through a low-rank expansion of its non-separable two-point kernel contracted mode-by-mode with the general-$m$ prolate Neumann Coulomb—so the entire $2×2$ CI energy assembles deterministically; for the cusp-correct geminal $f = r e^{-\gamma r}$ its correlation energy matches a same-geminal variational Monte-Carlo reference to sub-mHa, and the energy lies above the exact value (variational) (Sec. (ref)).

title: The Hyperspherical Lattice: Two-Electron Atoms as Coupled Channel Graphs
abstract: The natural geometry principle states that every separable quantum system has a natural lattice—the label set and channel structure of the coordinates in which separation occurs. For atoms, this is the label set of Fock's three-sphere $S^3$ (Papers 0, 1, 7); for diatomic molecules, the prolate spheroid (Paper 11). Hyperspherical coordinates are the natural setting for a genuine three-body coalescence, where the nuclear and interelectronic singularities meet at a point. (Earlier versions took this motivation from Paper 12's reading of its H$_2$ residual as an electron-electron cusp limit; Paper 12 has since withdrawn that reading, and nothing below depends on it.) This paper introduces the hyperspherical lattice for helium. The original adiabatic solver obtains $E = -2.9052$ Ha with a single channel—nominally 0.05% from the exact $-2.9037$ Ha, but non-variational: it lies below the exact energy because the single-channel adiabatic approximation omits the positive diagonal Born–Oppenheimer correction. A 2D variational solver treating hyperradius and hyperangle simultaneously (Note added v2.6.0) achieves a properly variational $0.022%$ raw at $l_{\max} = 7$; adding the Schwartz partial-wave tail at $l_{\max} = 4$ gives $0.020%$, still above the exact energy. A separate fixed-exponent configuration interaction in the hydrogenic $(n,l,m)$ basis at $k = Z$, with exact rational Slater integrals and zero free parameters, reaches $1.88%$ above the exact energy at $n_{\max} = 7$ with helium's physical Hamiltonian—a floor set by the missing continuum of the fixed-$k$ bound-state basis, not by the cusp. The hyperspherical lattice is structurally the same kind of object as the atomic $S^3$ lattice and the molecular prolate spheroidal lattice, but with one key generalization: it is a coupled-channel expansion in which the angular eigenvalue problem depends parametrically on the hyperradius, so that the channel functions vary with $R$. This coupled-channel structure has the form of a fiber bundle and provides the mathematical prototype for electron-nuclear coupling in molecules. As a demonstration of the framework's end-to-end capability, we combine the prolate spheroidal electron lattice with a nuclear lattice to produce ab initio rovibrational frequencies for H$_2$ with zero experimental spectroscopic input: the fundamental vibrational frequency $\nu_{01} = 4123$ cm$^{-1}$ (0.9% error) and the rotational constant $B_e = 59.3$ cm$^{-1}$ (2.6% error), computed from first principles using only nuclear charges and masses.

title: The Level 4 Natural Geometry: Two-Center Two-Electron Molecules in Molecule-Frame Hyperspherical Coordinates
abstract: The natural geometry hierarchy assigns each separable quantum system a coordinate system in which Coulomb singularities become boundary conditions and the problem becomes sparse and discrete: $S^3$ for hydrogen (Paper 7; there the discrete object is the exact label set of the $S^3$ harmonics, not an edge-Laplacian discretization, which does not converge), prolate spheroidal for H$_2^+$ (Paper 11), and hyperspherical for helium (Paper 13). The two-center, two-electron molecule H$_2$ combines all five Coulomb singularities; its leading geometry is prolate spheroidal (Paper 12). As the structural $N$-electron generalization, we introduce molecule-frame hyperspherical coordinates $(R_e,α,\theta_1,\theta_2,\Phi)$ parameterized by the dimensionless ratio $\rho = R/(2R_e)$, where $R$ is the internuclear distance and $R_e$ the electronic hyperradius. The electron–electron cusp appears at $α=π/4$, $\theta_{12}=0$, independent of molecular geometry, where in prolate spheroidal coordinates the same locus is not a coordinate surface. That is a structural difference in where the cusp sits, and—see below—it does not translate into an accuracy advantage. The molecular charge function depends on $(R,R_e)$ only through $\rho$, so it can be cached on a one-dimensional $\rho$ grid; the angular eigenvalues themselves depend on both $\rho$ and $R_e$. A coupled-channel expansion in body-frame partial waves $(l_1,m_1,l_2,m_2)$ with $l_1+l_2$ even (gerade symmetry) and $m_1+m_2=0$, solved with a two-dimensional $(R_e,α)$ solver that avoids the adiabatic approximation, recovers 96.0% of the exact dissociation energy $D_e$ at $l_{\max}=6$ with $\sigma$ and $π$ channels (61 channels) on a hyperradial grid with inner wall $R_{e,\min} = 0.3$ bohr; the Schwartz cusp tail at this truncation is $0.03$ mHa ($0.02$ percentage points). That wall is not converged: at $l_{\max}=4$ moving it to $0.05$ bohr raises the recovered $D_e$ from $94.1%$ to $96.9$–$97.3%$, depending on the hyperradial grid. The $96.0%$ is not compared against Paper 12: Paper 12's $\sigma$-only $92.4%$ lacks the $π$ channels included here, and its $|m| \le 1$ result ($99.1%$) differs from the ones here in truncation, cusp treatment and solver class alike, so no coordinate-system advantage is claimed in either direction. The framework is extended to heteronuclear diatomics (HeH$^+$, $Z_A=2$, $Z_B=1$) via a charge-center origin shift and removal of the gerade constraint; the adiabatic solver gives 93.1% of the exact $D_e$ at $l_{\max}=4$ ($\sigma{+}π$, 57 channels), a non-variational over-binding: the 2D treatment at the same truncation and inner wall recovers only ${\sim}5%$, the absolute energy error ($2.4%$) being comparable to the small $0.075$ Ha binding. The solver has a double-adiabatic coupled-channel structure—nuclear coordinates as outer slow variable, hyperradius as inner slow variable, angular channels as fast variables—generalizing the single-adiabatic expansion of Paper 13.

title: Composed Natural Geometries for Core-Valence Diatomics: LiH and BeH^+ from Natural-Geometry Solvers
abstract: The natural geometry hierarchy assigns each separable quantum system a coordinate system where Coulomb singularities become boundary conditions: $S^3$ for atoms (Paper 7), prolate spheroids for H$_2^+$ and H$_2$ (Papers 11, 12), hyperspherical for He (Paper 13), with molecule-frame hyperspherical coordinates as the structural two-electron treatment of H$_2$ that composition builds on (Paper 15). Systems with core electrons resist a single natural geometry because core and valence electrons occupy different length scales. We introduce composed natural geometries—fiber bundles where each electron group inhabits its own natural coordinate system, connected by screening functions and Phillips–Kleinman pseudopotentials built from the core wavefunction plus one empirical atomic input (the neutral atom's first ionization energy), with the barrier-width formula chosen among four candidates by comparison with the LiH equilibrium bond length. For LiH ($Z_A=3$, $Z_B=1$, 4 electrons): the Li$^+$ $1s^2$ core is solved via Level 3 hyperspherical (Paper 13), yielding $Z_{\rm eff}(r)$ and pseudopotential parameters; the two valence electrons are solved via Level 4 molecule-frame hyperspherical (Paper 15) with $Z_{\rm eff}$ injection; the potential energy surface is scanned via a $\rho$-collapse adiabatic method that reduces per-$R$-point cost to seconds. Results: $R_{\rm eq} = 3.22$ bohr (6.9% error vs. experiment 3.015, improved from 17% in LCAO), $\omega_e = 1465$ cm$^{-1}$ (4.2% error vs. 1406). The $l$-dependent PK variant reduces the $R_{\rm eq}$ error further, to 5.3%—the figure quoted as this paper's headline elsewhere in the corpus; 6.9% is the plain channel-blind PK. Total wall time is ${\sim}4$ minutes per molecule on commodity hardware. The same formula transfers to BeH$^+$ ($Z_A=4$) with no per-molecule tuning, giving a bound ion whose $R_{\rm eq}$ is 30% long.

title: Toward PK-Free Molecular Hamiltonians: Two-Center Sturmian Integrals and Coupled Composition
abstract: The composed natural geometry framework (Paper 17) constructs molecular Hamiltonians by partitioning electrons into single-center blocks and coupling them via Phillips–Kleinman (PK) pseudopotentials. This produces structurally sparse qubit Hamiltonians—a Pauli count exactly linear in the qubit count across molecules at fixed basis, $N_{\mathrm{Pauli}} = 27.90 × Q$, with $51×$–$317×$ fewer terms than equal-qubit Gaussian baselines (Paper 14; the retired pair-diagonal rule gave $O(Q^{2.5})$ and 51–1{,}712$×$)—but PK limits accuracy to 5.3–19.4% equilibrium bond length error. PK has resisted improvement: six modification attempts have failed (v2.0.6–23), and the overcounting diverges at higher angular momentum. We report a negative result (Track CB, v2.0.37): replacing PK with explicit cross-block electron-electron integrals without corresponding cross-center nuclear attraction integrals produces an unbalanced Hamiltonian (29% error, worse than PK's 15%). The root cause is identified: two-center one-body integrals $\langle \psi_{nlm}^A | V_B | \psi_{n'l'm'}^A \rangle$, where an orbital on center $A$ feels the nuclear potential of center $B$, are required for energy balance but absent from the single-center framework. We observe that these missing integrals are closely related to the Shibuya–Wulfman integrals of the Coulomb Sturmian literature [ref], which are computed via Fock's momentum-space projection onto $S^3$—the same conformal map that underlies the GeoVac framework (Paper 7). The mathematical foundation is therefore already in place. We review the convergence properties of the Shibuya–Wulfman expansion, identify the Coulomb resolution technique [ref] as a potentially faster alternative, and outline the ``coupled composition'' architecture that would result from incorporating two-center integrals. If the angular expansion converges in few terms at molecular bond lengths, the coupled Hamiltonian would be PK-free, structurally sparse, and significantly more accurate than the current composed framework. This paper presents the balanced coupled architecture, documents its mathematical foundations, and reports computational benchmarks across three molecules (LiH, BeH$_2$, H$_2$O). We report computational results from the first three phases. The convergence concern is resolved: the multipole expansion of the cross-center potential terminates exactly at $L_{\max} = 2l_{\max}$ by Gaunt selection rules (33 one-body terms at $n_{\max}=2$). The balanced Hamiltonian has 2{,}726 Pauli terms (Conjecture 1 holds in its ratio form only; see Sec. (ref)). Four-electron FCI gives a PES minimum with $R_{\rm eq}$ error of 7.0%, the only minimum among the four coupling schemes tested: the other three have $R$-independent one-body and electron-repulsion integrals, so their energies are a constant plus $3/R$ and cannot bind. No dissociation energy is defined: the balanced electron repulsion is also built $R$-independent, and past the minimum the curve keeps rising instead of approaching the separated atoms (Conjecture 2 not confirmed in strict sense, but the comparison crosses FCI regimes). At $n_{\max} = 3$ ($Q = 84$), single-point FCI gives 0.20% energy error (down from 1.8%) with analytical integrals (incomplete gamma functions, machine precision), the error decreasing through $n_{\max}=3$; at $n_{\max}=4$ the model crosses past exact (over-binding), so the fixed-geometry error is not monotonically improvable either. The $R_{\rm eq}$ drift is structural to the block decomposition ($+0.053$ then $+0.023$ bohr at the two available steps— decelerating, not a constant rate; the PK solver's drift, $+0.30$–$0.37$ bohr per unit $l_{\max}$ in Paper 17, is in a different truncation parameter and is not directly comparable), not numerical. It is, however, not a physics wall: a companion all-electron prolate-spheroidal treatment with an $R$-accurate analytic atom-centered core resolves it to $R_{\rm eq} = +0.2%$ (the corpus's best LiH geometry) and, with a rigorous VMC-over-FCI treatment (a two-body Jastrow on the analytic-orbital FCI state), reaches a variational energy of $-8.047$ Ha—$15$ mHa below the $-8.032$ orbital ceiling and safely above the exact $-8.0705$. A deterministic, resolution-of-identity–free explicit-$r_{12}$ treatment on the same $π$-containing reference, with a cusp-correct Slater geminal, improves this to $-8.0490$ Ha (variational, cross-checked by VMC of the same trial function to $0.16$ mHa); relaxing the CI coefficients alongside the geminal lowers it to $-8.0516$ Ha, and adding electron–nucleus factors on the Li core, built from the core orbital itself with no new parameter, to $-8.0585$ Ha. An additive-F12 estimate places the near-chemical target at $\approx-8.062$ Ha; the remaining gap is not electron–electron–nucleus correlation, which is worth $\lesssim3$ mHa here. The atom-centered core turns out to be a convenience rather than a necessity: a pure prolate product basis also represents it, at the cost of hundreds of primitives. The prolate route buys energy per qubit, not sparsity. Its first qubit Hamiltonian ($Q=20$) has $8{,}370$ Pauli terms, level with an equal-size Gaussian set and ten times the composed count at $Q=30$, at an energy $19$ mHa better than that Gaussian set. Together these results locate the balanced drift specifically in the frozen/parameter-free core rather than in the coupled architecture itself.

title: Angular Sparsity Is an Atomic-Sector Property: The Abelian Residue of Multi-Center Bonding
abstract: The GeoVac program builds molecular Hamiltonians from atom-centered hydrogenic blocks (screened $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ per block, not shared-$p_{0}$ Coulomb–Sturmian — a design choice, not a theorem: Papers 8–9 establish $R$-independence only under the imposed single-$n$ $D$-matrix premise (Paper 8, Remark ``Scope: the overlap premise is imposed, not generic''), and the genuine cross-$n$ Coulomb–Sturmian overlap escapes it; a validated two-centre Coulomb–Sturmian H$_2$ CI binds, Paper 60) whose angular matrix elements are generated from quantum-number labels by Gaunt selection, with no spatial quadrature. This yields structurally sparse qubit Hamiltonians—838 Pauli terms for LiH at $Q = 30$, exactly linear in $Q$ across molecules at fixed basis (Paper 14)—at the cost of a documented binding failure for second-row diatomics (the W1e wall, Papers 19/20 [ref]). We settle the question of whether that trade was necessary. Using exact rational two-center machinery (Mulliken auxiliary functions $A_n$/$B_n$ for overlaps; a hydrogenic eigen-trick for cross-center one-body terms, certified by an exact bra/ket identity holding entrywise), we census the genuine bare tensor $(S, h, g)$ for a real fragment pair and find: [MEASURED] the Gaunt $l$-selection rule does not survive cross-center evaluation, while the axial $m$-rule does; cross-center one-body entries reach $0.80$ Ha—bond scale, not perturbative. [COUNTED] the symmetry-permitted electron-repulsion density inflates $13.8×$ over the builder at $n_{\max} = 2$ and $15.0×$ at $n_{\max} = 3$; the $n_{\max} = 2$ figure is independently corroborated numerically ($29.8%$ measured against $29.4%$ counted), the $n_{\max} = 3$ figure is counted only. We give the mechanism [INTERNAL THEOREM]: $m$ labels the abelian symmetry shared by both centers (rotation about the internuclear axis is one global one-parameter group, so $m$ is a common label), while $l$ labels irreducible representations of a rotation group attached to a single center. The intersection of the two centers' rotation groups is exactly the axial $U(1)$, whose character group is $\mathbb{Z}$ by Pontryagin duality. Abelian selection rules are additive charge conservation and survive; non-abelian Clebsch–Gordan selection requires the full sphere and does not. The surviving cross-center angular rule is therefore the one generated by the common axial subgroup, which is readable from the molecular point group in advance. Two scope statements, since the title is shorter than the claim. ``Abelian residue'' names what survives cross-center among the continuous per-center labels—not everything that survives: same-center Gaunt selection persists from the full per-center $SO(3)$, and the largest group fixing both nuclei is $C_{\infty v}$, which is non-abelian and does yield usable label structure (its $\sigma_v$ reflection is the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ we use as the tapering baseline). And the mechanism is classical, not ours: the intersection rule is Curie's principle (1894), the reading of surviving labels as residual-subgroup irreducibles is descent in symmetry after Bethe (1929), and the character step is elementary Pontryagin duality. What is new here is the target— symmetry descent aimed at the sparsity of the two-center integral tensor rather than at spectroscopic level splittings—together with the census that quantifies it. Two re-readings follow. First, the $17.9×$ Pauli inflation previously attributed to Löwdin orthogonalization (v4.73.1) was not, in the bulk, orthogonalization's price: the genuine tensor's own permitted density inflates by the same order ($\sim 15×$) before any transformation, so Löwdin was paying a bill that was largely already owed. Second [OBSERVATION], four previously attempted relocations of the non-orthogonality—into the operator, into a dual basis, into a high-symmetry embedding, into device-measured many-body overlaps—each moved the cost without reducing it, because the cost measures the physical asymmetry of a two-center problem. A fifth, measured here, is the sharpest: enabling equivalent-atom-swap tapering reduces the qubit saving ($\mathrm{BeH_2}$ $12 \to 9$, $\mathrm{N_2}$ $22 \to 19$, $\mathrm{F_2}$ $22 \to 15$) while inflating the Pauli count $2.3$–$3.6×$, because the swap rotation merges per-block abelian gradings into joint stabilizers. A permutation identifies blocks, and identifying blocks destroys the per-block labels that generate the sparsity. We close with a demonstration [PANEL-VERIFIED]: all-electron 12-electron NaH, the framework's hardest documented failure, binds at $R_{\rm eq} = 3.736 a_0$ ($+4.8%$ vs experiment; the coarse-grid dissociation-scan well minimum, now test-backed) with $91.1%$ of in-basis FCI binding from three fragment-native determinants, once the integrals are genuine end-to-end—with fewer correlation degrees of freedom than the runs that failed, which is what makes the inference go through. This localizes W1e to the Hamiltonian specification rather than the correlation treatment on this system. The demonstration deliberately forfeits the sparsity: it makes no sparsity claim. [SYMBOLIC + MEASURED] Separately, the diatomic integrals are made quadrature-free: the minimal-basis H$_2$ FCI energy is certified to $60$ digits with symbolic $\tau$-series termination, its entire potential curve $E(R)$ is a single closed-form expression in $\{\exp, E_{1}, \log, \gamma\}$ with certified $R_{\rm eq}$, $D_{e}$ and $k$, and the heteronuclear LiH case reaches $30$ digits net of an explicit tail bound (a campaign value; its regression test is owed). A by-product bears on the continuous theory the census borrows from: the radial integral at the core of the two-center direct-Coulomb $(AA|BB)$ repulsion closes in elementary form (weight one, $π$-free, no dilogarithm), so that block is not merely counted but decided—all $195$ permitted entries proven nonzero by Lindemann–Weierstrass separation.

title: The Three-Center Electron-Repulsion Integral Is an Elliptic Bessel Moment: A Genus-One Radial Core at the Third Center in Momentum-Space Slater Theory
abstract: Two-center electron-repulsion integrals over Slater-type orbitals close in elementary functions plus the exponential integral, the logarithm, and Euler's $\gamma$—a genus-zero transcendence class—which is why the two-center problem has been solved since Roothaan and Ruedenberg. The genuine three-center integral has resisted a closed form for seventy years, and the standard verdict is that it is simply hard: reduce it to an infinite series or a one-dimensional quadrature and be done. We give it a structural reading instead. Evaluating the two-electron three-center integral $(XY|XZ)$ over $1s$ orbitals in momentum space—the Fock projection under which Coulomb–Sturmians become hyperspherical harmonics, the setting native to the Averys' generalized-Sturmian program—the three centers enter as three phases rather than three foci, so the coordinate obstruction (prolate spheroidal coordinates admit exactly two foci) dissolves. [MEASURED] The resulting momentum integral reproduces the exact integral (agreement $1.9×10^{-14}$ with McMurchie–Davidson on the same Gaussian fits; with the true Slater density, $4.3×10^{-7}$ against the fitted reference, which itself sits $7×10^{-8}$ above the Slater value), and its angular part collapses to a single spherical Bessel kernel. [MEASURED / classical] What remains—the radial content—is a two-scale Bessel moment whose period is a complete elliptic integral (verified to 31 digits), living on the genus-one curve $y^{2}=(c_{1}k^{2}+1)(c_{2}k^{2}+1)$; it degenerates to the genus-zero two-center case exactly on the diagonal $c_{1}=c_{2}$. [SYMBOLIC + MEASURED] The one-mass slice is the Laplace transform of the elliptic differential—an elliptic deformation of the Bessel $K_{0}$, reducing to $K_{0}(D)$ when one scale decouples ($\rho\to0$) and to the complete elliptic integral $K$ at zero separation—and satisfies an explicit fourth-order Picard–Fuchs equation with polynomial coefficients, whose characteristic exponents are the four branch points of the curve. [OBSERVATION] This places a molecular integral inside the modern theory of Bessel moments and two-mass elliptic Feynman integrals; a targeted literature search finds that connection unmade in either field. [OPEN] We do not give the finite closed form, and we show the natural route to it is obstructed: the elliptic-dilogarithm (unequal-mass sunrise) mechanism does not engage, because the modulus Picard–Fuchs source is not an elementary subtopology but lies in the integral's own Gauss–Manin $D$-module—the branch-point boundary that would supply the sunrise's tadpole vanishes identically. [OBSERVATION] The object is therefore an apparently unclaimed elliptic transcendent one level above the elliptic-dilogarithm tower, a period of a rank-four irregular connection. [SYMBOLIC + MEASURED] That connection is irreducible—it is the Fourier–Laplace transform of an irreducible connection, and its monodromy admits no invariant coordinate subspace—so no closed form arises through factorization; [OPEN] whether the irreducible object admits a transcendental closed form we leave open. The message is not a solution but a relocation: the third center does not make the radial core messier within the two-center class, it raises the radial core's transcendence one genus, past the reach of the sunrise's elliptic-dilogarithm mechanism. [MEASURED] The integrated three-center value leaves the two-center class too, as a function of the bond angle: its bond-angle operator, built from exact coefficients modulo primes, keeps a piece of order six with no first-order factor at two geometries, where a two-center-class form would factor completely (assuming its constants independent; the class of the value at one geometry is not decided). The rungs beyond the third center—a fourth center, the three-electron chain's K3 surface, four linked densities and the first period beyond elliptic ones, and the ring of three—are taken up in Paper 63 [ref], which places every exponential-type orbital's integral in the $D$-module of the $1s$ one.

title: The Generalized-Sturmian Secular Equation Block-Encodes Without a Metric: A Quantum-Algorithm Analysis, Metric-Free for Atoms and a Conditioning Frontier for Molecules
abstract: Central result. In Avery's isoenergetic (potential-weighted) posing, the atomic Coulomb–Sturmian secular equation is a standard, metric-free eigenproblem—an apparently novel quantum-encoding target, with both documented cost-risks of the genre (metric conditioning; an outer energy search) structurally absent—whereas the naive $L^{2}$ posing of the same basis inflates the cost instead. Its block-encoding $1$-norm grows more slowly than the configuration count over every basis we can compute, and more slowly as the basis grows. That advantage, however, belongs to the basis-growth rule rather than to the construction: it holds when $l_{\max}$ is fixed and higher-$n$ configurations are added, and weakens when the basis is grown as full hydrogenic shells — there the total exponent rises toward $1$ ($0.867\to0.911$) while remaining below it, and only the pure-number block $T'$ itself goes superlinear. The cheap rule also carries an accuracy floor, whose mechanism we locate exactly: the metric-free form holds iff the basis scale is locked to the eigenvalue, $\lambda=p_\kappa=\sqrt{-2E}$, and that lock is not the variational optimum. Solving the same span variationally with the scale freed reaches chemical accuracy, but hands back both of the cost risks named above — the $L^{2}$ metric returns, and the scale becomes an outer search — along with the encoding advantage itself ($1$-norm growth from $K^{\gvq{p60_freescale_set_sonly}{0.72}}$ to $K^{2.75}$ on the $s$-only comparison ladder, $\mathrm{cond}(S)\sim K^{0.94}$). The absence of those two risks and the presence of the floor are therefore not independent virtues and defects but one structural fact. The floor is moreover a ground-state pathology rather than a property of the method: because $\|M\|_1$ does not depend on which root is extracted, every $^{1}S$ state costs the same to encode, and at the largest basis where both roots were computed, $K=452$, the ground state sits $\gvq{p60_gnd_ratio_k452}{4.28}×$ above chemical accuracy while $2 ^{1}S$ sits $\gvq{p60_exc_ratio_k452}{1.08}×$ above it; and on the $s$-only ladder at $K=105$ the posing cost falls by $4.3×$, $3.0×$ and $2.6×$ across the first three rungs of the $^{1}S$ ladder. The result is therefore a measured trade-off between cost growth, attainable accuracy and which state is targeted, not an unconditional efficiency claim. The development follows. A recurring intuition in quantum simulation is that a Coulomb–Sturmian / hyperspherical basis is well suited to a quantum computer, because its angular matrix elements are exact algebraic numbers (square roots of rationals) generated on the device from quantum-number labels rather than loaded as a classically-computed tensor; only the one-dimensional radial content need be shipped in. We test the load-bearing obstruction to that idea—the cost of encoding the basis—and find it turns sharply on how the basis is posed. [MEASURED] Encoded naively, in the ordinary $L^2$ Schrödinger framework, the genuine shared-scale Coulomb–Sturmian basis is $L^2$-non-orthogonal; a second-quantized (Jordan–Wigner) encoding must Löwdin-orthogonalize it, and the LCU $1$-norm $\lambda$ then inflates as $\lambda\sim Q^{3.3}$ (versus $Q^{1.2}$ for an orthonormal hydrogenic basis), driven by the dense $S^{-1/2}$ that Löwdin orthogonalization introduces as the basis members grow increasingly non-orthogonal. [ESTABLISHED, from Avery's formulation] The generalized-Sturmian isoenergetic reformulation removes this obstruction for atoms: posed in the potential-weighted metric in which the Coulomb–Sturmians are orthonormal, the atomic secular equation is a standard (metric-free) eigenproblem $[ \mathrm{diag}(Z R_\nu)+T'-p_\kappa\mathbb{1} ]B=0$ whose eigenvalues are the scaling parameters $p_\kappa=\sqrt{-2E}$ directly and whose interelectron matrix $T'$ is a matrix of pure numbers, independent of $p_\kappa$, of energy, and of $Z$. [MEASURED] We implement it, validate it against helium (a single Goscinskian configuration reproduces the textbook variational value $-2.847$ Ha; adding configurations lowers the energy monotonically through the $s$, $+p$ and $spdf$ sectors—past the locked $s$-sector value $\gvq{p60_he_chain_s_k55}{-2.8745}$ Ha to $\gvq{p60_he_chain_spdf_k164}{-2.8964}$ Ha, toward the exact non-relativistic $-2.90372$ Ha), and measure the decisive quantity: the block-encoding $1$-norm of the secular matrix grows more slowly than the matrix dimension, $\|M\|_1\sim K^{\gvq{p60_onenorm_exponent}{0.82}}$ over the computed range $K=74$–$164$ (full $s\!+\!p\!+\!d\!+\!f$, helium; $K^{\gvq{p60_onenorm_exponent_sonly}{0.73}}$ $s$-only)—the opposite of the naive inflation. The exponent is a fit over a window and not an asymptotic regime: its local slope falls monotonically with $K$ (Sec. (ref)), it moves with the nuclear charge, and it belongs to the fixed-$l_{\max}$ growth rule rather than to the construction. [OBSERVATION] A targeted prior-art search finds no existing quantum algorithm combining a Sturmian basis, a quantum eigenvalue routine, and the isoenergetic inversion; the two documented cost risks for such an algorithm—metric conditioning and an outer energy search—are both absent in the atomic case (no metric; the eigenvalues $p_\kappa$ give the energies directly, $E=-p_\kappa^2/2$). [MEASURED] For molecules the Shibuya–Wulfman metric returns and the problem is again generalized; we measure its conditioning and find it, on the $s$-sector, uniformly better than the $L^2$ overlap—its intra-center block is exactly the identity—and markedly better at larger internuclear separation, but still growing with basis size through the inter-center coupling. [MEASURED] Every conditioning law below is measured on the $s$-sector shared-scale basis; on a full $\sigma$ basis ($\ell>0$) the growth is exponential in the number of shells, in the gerade sector too, and the one-center set approaches completeness in the molecular metric, so the gerade, preconditioner and one-direction levers do not transfer as stated; no preconditioner of that kind exists there, because the two-center metric is a finite section of an operator with spectrum $\{0,2\}$, and dropping the redundant directions is the remedy that works, at the price of a classical eigendecomposition of the one-electron metric. [PRIOR ART] On the $s$-sector the growth law is not new: the band-limited concentration rate $1-\sigma_{\max}\propto(kR)^2/n^2$, asymptotic exponent $2$, is the Kac–Murdock–Szeg\H{o} asymptotic, and what is ours is the identification of the Shibuya–Wulfman metric as such a finite section (the fitted window exponents $1.85$/$1.97$ are pre-asymptotic readings). [MEASURED] The same cross-center singular spectrum carries the composition-wall commutator, whose norm saturates at $\tfrac12$. [RESOURCE MODEL] Turning this into a block-encoding count for $\mathrm{H}_2^+$ (validated to bind, $1.3%$ $s$-only), the payoff is the gerade/ungerade lever: the $\sigma_g$ ground state lives in the gerade sector, whose $s$-sector conditioning is flat—and flat at an exact constant of the sinc symbol, $2/(1+\min_x j_0(x))=2.555041\ldots$, independent of $R$ and of basis size—so the ground-state metric penalty does not grow with basis size—a ${\sim}60×$ reduction versus the full metric and $10^3$–$10^4×$ smaller than a standard Gaussian metric for the same problem (a metric-versus-metric ratio that scales with the Gaussian exponent spread, hence illustrative rather than a fixed factor), at ${\sim}30$ qubits. [MEASURED] The penalty also does not compound with electron number: the metric is discharged once at the one-electron molecular-orbital construction, after which the many-electron secular equation carries an identity metric—the metric cost is one-electron, not $N$-electron. [MEASURED] A third lever removes the conditioning cost outright where it applies: the ill-conditioning is a symbol zero of known order and location, so a band-Toeplitz preconditioner bounds $\mathrm{cond}$ flat in basis size, and—unlike the gerade lever—it does not require equivalent centers, reaching water's $A_1$ block (bounded at $44$ out to $N=192$, against a raw $N^{1.97}$), provided the band is aligned to the symbol's null direction: in the unrotated frame the same band is $106×$ worse than no treatment at all. [RESOURCE MODEL] A direct block-encoding of the preconditioned metric then takes the penalty from $n^3$ to $n$ (the circulant-embedded circuit is analysed, not compiled). [OPEN] The atomic case is a clean, apparently novel, metric-free quantum secular equation; the molecular case is a frontier on which the conditioning axis is removable on $s$-sector shared-scale bases at $M=2$ and non-collinear $M=3$, the locality cost is capped by the symbol's other pole, and the $\ell$-block sparsity loss is structural and not a conditioning effect at all. [MEASURED] Its remaining question—whether the $N$-electron $1$-norm stays sublinear as it does for atoms—is open, and we identify the obstruction: the atomic sublinearity rides on a diagonal nuclear matrix $T^0=Z R_\nu$ that is single-center-specific, and a validated two-center CI (dissociating $\mathrm{H}_2$ correctly) has a standard block-encoding $1$-norm growing polynomially ($\sim n_{\rm orb}^{2.2}$), with no sublinear behavior. The real molecular savings are the metric levers (the band-Toeplitz preconditioner, the gerade sector, large separation, one-electron-only metric), not a sublinear matrix — and the first two are $s$-sector results, while on a full $\sigma$ basis large separation only delays the growth. We do not demonstrate the algorithm on hardware; this is a structural and resource analysis.

title: Water at Twenty-Four Functions: Slater-Type Bases Set on the Free Atom Against cc-pVDZ, With the Qubit Cost
abstract: Central result. At a fixed basis size of twenty-four functions, the size of cc-pVDZ on water, we ask how much of the Gaussian basis's correlated energy a one-centre Slater-type design recovers when its exponents are set on the free atoms, and what that costs in qubit resources. [MEASURED] A Slater double-zeta-plus-polarization basis built by cc-pVDZ's own design rule sits $40.7 \mathrm{mHa}$ below cc-pVDZ at frozen-core CCSD(T), of which $28.8 \mathrm{mHa}$ is self-consistent field. [MEASURED, pre-registered] cc-pVDZ is built for systematic convergence, not for the lowest energy at its size; of three published Gaussian bases of the same size, ANO-R1 is $23.6 \mathrm{mHa}$ below cc-pVDZ, and the Slater DZP's margin over it is $17.1 \mathrm{mHa}$. [MEASURED, negative] Every exponential kit with fixed or shared exponents loses: the hydrogenic $Z/n$ rule by $196 \mathrm{mHa}$, a single Coulomb–Sturmian scale per atom by more than one hartree, and a two-scale Sturmian kit by $130 \mathrm{mHa}$; the hydrogenic loss is the fixed radial node structure, not the decay rate.
