[MEASURED, pre-registered] Releasing the oxygen exponents one at a time, every value set by the free oxygen atom's radial Hartree–Fock energy with nothing tuned on water, closes that gap: with five oxygen exponents the water energy lands $3.1 \mathrm{mHa}$ below cc-pVDZ, and $7.0 \mathrm{mHa}$ below with hydrogen exponents set on H$_2$. The split of the $2p$ from the $3p$ exponent carries $0.900$ of the water gain, as it carries $0.902$ of the atom's; the water gain is $0.516$ of the atom's. Both were predicted before the water energies were computed. The one non-monotone rung is diagnosed: its correlation loss transfers from the atom one to one and is mostly a $3d$ exponent the atomic objective never sees, while its Hartree–Fock gain is two opposite pieces that cancel on water. [MEASURED] The Jordan–Wigner Pauli count is the same for every twenty-four-function basis, $107 382$ terms on 46 frozen-core qubits, because in canonical orbitals without degenerate pairs it is fixed by the orbital count and the $C_{2v}$ pattern; across this paper's own kits the 1-norm rises with accuracy, from 405 to 706 Ha (the one-scale Sturmian aside), but not across Gaussian families: ANO-R1 is more accurate than cc-pVDZ at 625 Ha. Caps. One geometry and one method per molecule; the ladder and the native kits are water only. The water-tuned Slater basis stays $34 \mathrm{mHa}$ below the best atom-set rung, and $21.7$ mHa below once the $3d$ is also set on the atom's correlated energy (pre-registered; water then lands $19.0$ mHa below cc-pVDZ, still $4.7 \mathrm{mHa}$ above ANO-R1). [MEASURED, pre-registered] At matched accuracy the Gaussian cost depends on the family. In the cc-pV family aug-cc-pVDZ at 41 functions stays $8.0 \mathrm{mHa}$ short of the Slater DZP while already costing $9.2×$ the Pauli terms. In the ANO family a 35-function truncation of ANO-R2 is $6.2 \mathrm{mHa}$ below it, at $4.7×$ the Pauli terms and $2.3×$ the 1-norm on 68 qubits against 46 (registered as falling short; the prediction missed). The measured matched-accuracy cost is therefore at most $4.7×$ the terms; ANO-R1 at 24 functions falls short, and the crossing between 24 and 35 functions was not located. [MEASURED, pre-registered] The same rule on hydrogen fluoride, a second molecule, repeats both cc-pV findings: the Slater DZP is $59.5 \mathrm{mHa}$ below cc-pVDZ at nineteen functions with the same Pauli count, and aug-cc-pVDZ is still short at $9.3×$ the terms; the ANO family was not run there. [MEASURED, pre-registered; STOP] A ring of six hydrogens, with no core, does not: the Slater DZP is only $3.5$ mHa below cc-pVDZ at thirty functions, and one more Gaussian polarization shell at 48 functions already beats it, so the cc-pV matched-accuracy margin is a property of these two molecules, not of exponential functions. Nothing here is a GeoVac lattice structure: the bases are tuned exponential functions evaluated through Gaussian fits, and the angular sparsity of the one-centre framework does not enter.

title: Bond Sphere: Diatomic Molecules as S^3 and their Natural Sturmian Basis
abstract: A diatomic molecule is geometrically a single three-sphere $S^3$ with two weighted poles—the bond sphere—in which the internuclear distance $R$ encodes as a polar angle $\gamma$ via $\cos\gamma = (p_0^2 - p_R^2)/(p_0^2 + p_R^2)$ and, in a single-$n$ model, the cross-atom matrix elements are taken to be $SO(4)$ Wigner $D$-matrix elements evaluated at the bond rotation $e^{i\gamma A_y}$. Positive results: The bond sphere geometry is consistent, with the $\gamma(R)$ encoding, heteronuclear egg metric, and Runge–Lenz alignment following from $SO(4)$ representation theory. (A graph-partition ``kinetic membrane'' is also described; it is built on the graph Laplacian, which is not $SO(4)$-covariant, and its Fiedler-shift and Bader-analog claims are unverified.) The $D$-matrix enforces selection rules for $\sigma$-bonds: $D^2_{10,10}(\gamma) = 1$ and $D^2_{00,10}(\gamma) = 0$ for all $\gamma$. Negative theorem: In the molecular Sturmian basis with shared momentum scale $p_0$, with the between-centre overlap and potential blocks both taken as single-$n$ $D$-matrix elements and the same-centre blocks held constant, the one-electron Hamiltonian and overlap obey the two-term identity $H_{ij} = -\tfrac{1}{2}p_0^2 S_{ij} + (1-\beta_j)V_{ij}$, and their entire $R$-dependence is a single orthogonal $SO(4)$ congruence $D^{(n)}(\gamma(R))$ that cancels in the generalized eigenvalue problem: the eigenvalues are independent of $R$. In this single-$n$, shared-$p_0$ form, binding would require the $R$-dependent prolate spheroidal spectrum $\beta_k(R)$; but the genuine cross-$n$ Coulomb–Sturmian overlap and potential couple $n$, escape the theorem, and supply that $R$-dependence algebraically via Shibuya–Wulfman (Remark (ref)), so what is ruled out is this approximation, not Sturmian molecular binding. The continuous-geometry route—working in the label set and channel structure of prolate spheroidal coordinates, where the problem separates—is developed in the companion Paper 11 [ref].

title: Full configuration interaction in a hydrogenic basis on the S^3 label set: Multi-electron atoms via relational lattice indexing
abstract: We implement full configuration interaction (FCI) for multi-electron atoms in a hydrogenic basis on the $S^3$ label set $(n,l,m)$: the physical Hamiltonian is the diagonal hydrogenic one-body term plus two-electron integrals assembled by Slater–Condon rules from exact $R^k$ radial integrals and Gaunt angular coupling coefficients. For helium, the ground-state energy with the physical Hamiltonian converges monotonically to $-2.8476 Ha$ (1.93% error versus exact) at $n_{\max}=5$, above the Hartree–Fock limit: the fixed-exponent hydrogenic bound-state basis omits the continuum. For lithium, the energy converges to $-7.4007 Ha$ (1.03% error) at $n_{\max}=5$. Against strong baselines the comparison is unfavourable: the helium energy stays above the Hartree–Fock limit, which correlation-consistent Gaussian bases pass already at cc-pVDZ; only the one-function STO-3G basis is bettered. For beryllium (4 electrons), the solver achieves $E = -14.563 Ha$ (0.71% error) at $n_{\max}=4$ with $487{,}635$ determinants—the first four-electron calculation in this framework. For lithium hydride (4 electrons, first heteronuclear molecule), the $R$-independence of each atom's one-electron block makes the potential-energy surface monotonically attractive with no equilibrium geometry, and it does not return to the separated-atom energy at large $R$, so no binding energy is extracted. An excitation-driven direct CI algorithm following Knowles and Handy [ref] replaces the $O(N_{SD}^2)$ pairwise determinant loop with $O(N_{SD} × N_{connected})$ assembly, achieving a 45$×$ speedup for lithium. The Hamiltonian is assembled via a relational lattice index that maps Slater determinants to sparse matrix entries without evaluating continuous four-center integrals, achieving $>$99% sparsity at the largest basis sizes tested. These results establish hydrogenic-basis FCI on the $S^3$ label set as a working, if basis-limited, route for few-electron systems.

title: Full Configuration Interaction for Heteronuclear Diatomics in Concatenated Atom-Centred Bases: LiH as a Benchmark
abstract: We present a Topological LCAO architecture for heteronuclear full configuration interaction (FCI) within the GeoVac discrete graph framework. Two independent atom-centered hydrogenic lattices are concatenated into a bipartite molecular graph via Mulliken cross-nuclear attraction on the diagonal, Slater–Condon two-electron repulsion integrals with exact $R^k$ radial integrals and Gaunt coefficients, and STO-overlap bridges on the off-diagonal; the resulting one- and two-electron Hamiltonian is diagonalized in the full Slater determinant space (4 845 determinants for LiH at $n_{\max}=2$, where the results below are obtained; the solver also handles the 367 290 determinants of $n_{\max}=3$). For LiH the balanced Hamiltonian produces a monotonically attractive potential energy surface with no equilibrium geometry; at $n_{\max}=2$ the curve still lies 0.22 Ha below the separated-atom energy at $R=8$ bohr, so it does not dissociate to the atoms and no binding energy is extracted. The absence of a minimum is traced to the $R$-independence of the intra-atom one-electron block: unlike continuous quantum mechanics, each atom's hydrogenic diagonal $-Z^2/(2n^2)$ is fixed at construction and does not respond to inter-nuclear compression; the large-$R$ offset is not diagnosed here. A Fock-weighted kinetic correction, whose form is motivated by the energy-shell constraint $p_0^2 = Z^2/n^2$ of Paper 7 but whose overall scale $\lambda$ is a single fitted parameter (retained as a labeled qualitative diagnostic, not a zero-parameter result), partially restores the equilibrium by concentrating orthogonalization repulsion on compact core orbitals, giving $R_{\mathrm{eq}}\approx 3.7$ bohr at $\lambda=0.1$ ($n_{\max}=2$) without repairing the large-$R$ limit. A 29-version diagnostic arc (v0.9.8–v0.9.37) systematically tested and eliminated every competing hypothesis: basis set superposition error as a geometric driver, integral incompleteness, orbital exponent relaxation, the single-$n$, shared-$p_0$ SO(4) Sturmian bond sphere approximation, and Hamiltonian imbalance between cross-nuclear and electron repulsion orbital subspaces. In particular, Wigner $D$-matrix selection rules $D^{2}_{10,10}(\gamma)=1$ and $D^{2}_{00,10}(\gamma)=0$ are proven as structural results. The excitation-driven Direct CI solver achieves $O(N_{\mathrm{SD}}× N_{\mathrm{connected}})$ scaling, preserving the $O(V)$ character of the underlying graph Hamiltonian.

title: Counting Angular Momentum Labels by Isotropic Packing
abstract: [SYMBOLIC PROOF] We show that the angular momentum label set $(\ell, m)$ is counted exactly by a geometric construction: uniform-density packing of distinguishable states on concentric isotropic shells in two dimensions. Starting from two axioms—discrete binary distinguishability and geometric indifference (maximum entropy)—and the construction's structural choices (motivated, not forced), the construction yields per-shell angular capacities $2k-1$ for shell $k$, equal in count to the spherical harmonic basis $Y_{\ell m}$ with $\ell = k - 1$ and $m = -\ell, \ldots, +\ell$ (assigning the $m$ values to positions is a labelling choice). [OBSERVATION] The principal quantum number $n$ corresponds to a cumulative grouping of the first $n$ shells, producing the $n^2$ orbital count, but this grouping is not forced by the axioms alone. Similarly, the per-shell count carries a factor of 2 from the binary initialization ($N_{\mathrm{init}} = 2$), which we read as corresponding to spin multiplicity (a counting correspondence, not a derivation of spin). On the label set taken as a graph, the Laplacian splits into $\ell$-blocks (the edges change $n$ or $m$, never $\ell$) and so does not converge to the $S^3$ Laplacian—the spinless node set is the exact $S^3$ label set, on which $-\Delta_{S^3} = L^2 + A^2$ is the diagonal $SO(4)$ Casimir $n^2-1$—and [INTERNAL THEOREM] its top eigenvalue saturates the bipartite bound $\lambda_{\max} \to 2 d_{\max} = 8$ (attained in a mid-$\ell$ block, not in the $s$-wave block, whose own bound is 4), so that under a single matched scale $K_{\mathrm{vac}} = -1/16$ the extremal eigenvalue reaches the hydrogen ground-state energy—matched, not derived: the content that could have failed is the spectral bound, not the target the scale is matched to. \gvc{graph-s3-wall}{The per-shell spectrum $E_n = -Z^2/(2n^2)$ is not a function of the graph Laplacian}. On the labels it is the function $E_n = -Z^2/(2(C+1))$ of the diagonal Casimir $C = n^2-1$, i.e. the bound-state Hamiltonian is $H = -\tfrac{Z^2}{2}(1-\Delta_{S^3})^{-1}$, and that function is fixed by Fock's continuum projection: the eigenvalue $2π^2/n$ of the $S^3$ Coulomb kernel forces the focal length $p_0 = Z/n$, and the energy shell $p_0^2 = -2E$ then gives $E_n$ (Paper 7). [OBSERVATION] This angular cross-section recurs across the natural geometries of the Geometric Vacuum series as a basis label: the full $(\ell, m)$ labeling, with $2\ell+1$ states per $\ell$, labels the basis on $S^3$ for hydrogen, the per-electron partial waves of the hyperspherical treatment of helium, the angular channels of the molecule-frame hyperspherical treatment, and each fiber of the composed bundles ($\ell$ is a conserved quantum number only for the one-electron atom; elsewhere it is a channel label coupled by Gaunt coefficients); in the two-centre prolate-spheroidal geometry only $m$ survives as a label, because the $\eta$-separation replaces $\ell$ by a separation index that reduces to it only in the united-atom limit. This is Paper 0 in the series.

title: Spectral-Geometric Exchange Constants: Projecting Discrete Spectra onto Continuous Manifolds
abstract: Compact Lie groups have discrete unitary representations (Peter–Weyl theorem); the GeoVac label set exploits this discreteness directly. Transcendental conversion factors appear when these discrete representations are projected onto non-compact coordinate systems used for measurement. We classify these factors by the type of compactness mismatch they mediate—six exchange-constant tiers (intrinsic, conformal/calibration, embedding, algebraic-implicit, composition, inner-factor input data) plus the algebraic (no-exchange) case, seven categories in all, spanning the GeoVac hierarchy through Level 5 plus the almost-commutative inner factor—and identify them with Weyl–Selberg exchange constants of spectral geometry. The falsifiable claim: the transcendental content of any GeoVac observable is determined entirely by the type of projection linking the compact discrete description to the non-compact coordinate system (this strong, observable-indexed form is under strain from the H$_2$ dissociation energy and is not reconciled with the body's weaker, route-indexed Claim 4; see Sec. (ref)). Beyond the basis-level catalog, three theorems classify the spectral content of operators on round $S^3$: (Theorem 1) for the Camporesi–Higuchi $D$ against $D^2$, operator order is the primary discriminant of transcendental class (not for every second-order operator: $\nabla^*\nabla$ fails)—the squared Dirac operator $D^2$ produces $π^{\mathrm{even}}$ exclusively at every integer $s$, while the first-order Dirac operator $D$ produces odd-zeta content $ζ_R(2k{+}1)$ at odd $s$ (conjecturally outside $\mathbb{Q}(π)$;\ Apéry proved only that $ζ_R(3)$ is irrational); (Theorem 2) the full classification is three-axis, adding bundle type (scalar vs. spinor, modulating coefficients only) and diagram topology (free vs. parity-restricted, introducing Dirichlet $L$-values $G = \beta(2)$, $\beta(4)$ through the quarter-integer Hurwitz shift); (Theorem 3) the three components of the fine-structure-constant combination $K = π(B + F - \Delta)$ of Paper 2 [ref] have spectral homes of distinct type (finite Casimir trace, infinite Dirichlet series at the packing exponent, Dirac mode degeneracy on the spinor bundle);\ $B$ and $F$ share the (second-order, scalar) cell of the three-axis grid and differ by finite versus infinite summation, and $\Delta$ sits in the (first-order, spinor) cell. The combination rule—$K$ matches $α^{-1}$ to $4.8×10^{-7}$ relative, and $α$ approximately satisfies the cubic $α^3 - Kα + 1 = 0$ to $8.8×10^{-8}$—remains a numerical Observation without first-principles derivation. A complementary Observation (structural incommensurability) catalogues the meta-pattern: GeoVac observables that look unitary at the surface ($K$ itself; the two-loop Dirac spectral sum on $S^3$; zero structure of the GeoVac zeta) resolve under structural analysis into objects of different type (not always different cells of the three-axis grid:\ $K$'s $B$ and $F$ share one). No further unification is currently visible. The taxonomy is read (a census and a reading, not a classification) in terms of Mellin transforms of heat kernels: the free heat kernel produces $π^{\mathrm{even}}$ in its integer-$s$ spectral-zeta values (for $\Delta_{\mathrm{LB}}$ and $D^2$), restricting the spectrum to one parity class produces $L$-content, and operator order determines whether the Mellin integrand samples squared or raw eigenvalues. The taxonomy is $R$-independent, persisting in the flat-space limit via Weyl's law.

title: The Geometric Atom: the Hydrogen State Space as a Label Lattice
abstract: We study a discrete labelling of the hydrogen atom's bound-state space. The states $|n,\ell,m\rangle$ are indexed by a label lattice, drawn as a paraboloid (a visualization in which the depth coordinate $-1/n^2$ is placed by hand, not an output), on which the $SU(2)× SU(1,1)$ ladder operators act as sparse matrices. This single-particle model separates two kinds of content: (i) Algebraic exactness: [SYMBOLIC PROOF] \gvc{p1-ladder-exact}{Transition operators $T_\pm, L_\pm$ reproduce the Rydberg quantum numbers exactly from operator eigenvalues (a two-line commutator identity, checked in exact arithmetic): the $SU(1,1)$ element $N = -2[T_+, T_-]$ returns $n$ on the interior shells $n < n_{\max}$ (not on the truncated top shell), and $L^2$ returns $\ell(\ell+1)$ on every shell}; [PRIOR ART] on every shell, including the top one, the $SO(4)$ Casimir $\mathbf{L}^2 + \mathbf{A}^2 = n^2 - 1$ ($\mathbf{A}$ the energy-normalized Runge–Lenz vector) is exact on the labels (Fock [ref]). The energies $E_n = -1/(2n^2)$ are an imposed map from $n$ (Fock's energy shell $p_0^2 = -2E$, with $p_0 = Z/n$ fixed by Fock's kernel eigenvalue, Paper 7), not an output of the ladder operators; once Fock's kernel fixes the function, on the labels they are $E_n = -1/(2(C+1))$ of the Casimir $C = n^2-1$ (i.e. $H = -\tfrac12(1-\Delta_{S^3})^{-1}$ at $Z = 1$). (ii) Geometric artifacts: [MEASURED] A node-amplitude proxy for the $s/p$ gap is nonzero at finite lattice cutoff ($37%$ at $n_{\max}=5$, oscillating through $15.6%$ at $8$ and $1.7%$ at $10$ to $0.39%$ at $30$ on the binary production lattice; see the \S III QA note). [INTERNAL THEOREM] Its size tracks the residue of $n_{\max}$ modulo $3$ — exactly closed form on $n_{\max} \equiv 0$, and generically larger off it (the off-/on-branch ratio grows asymptotically as $n_{\max}/(\sqrt{3} π)$) — so the quoted endpoint sits on a favourable branch and the sequence is not evidence of convergence. The cutoff sweep from $n_{\max}=5$ to 30 shows this is a discretization artifact—a residue-controlled truncation effect (the $l$-blocks are disconnected and carry no degeneracy to lift)—that oscillates and reads $0.39%$ at $n_{\max}=30$ on the $n_{\max}\equiv 0 \pmod 3$ branch ($1.65%$ and $2.58%$ at $28$ and $29$): a proxy value, not a recovery of the Coulomb degeneracy, which belongs to the continuum operator (the graph's $l$-blocks are disconnected, so the graph has no $s/p$ degeneracy of its own). (iii) Geometric phase structure: [SYMBOLIC PROOF] The Berry phase vanishes identically for the real-valued transition operators; on the optional topological-weight lattice ($w = 1/(n_1 n_2)$) the edge-weight log-holonomy $\Theta(n) = -2\ln((n{+}1)/n) \sim n^{-1}$ measures the variation (a discrete gradient) of that weight function (on the binary production lattice and the CG-magnitude construction $\Theta \equiv 0$). This model describes only the electron's state space: it contains no electromagnetic coupling, and we find no trace of the fine structure constant $α$ in it (a companion paper [ref] records a separate numerical Observation about $α$, not a coupling mechanism).

title: Potential-Independent Angular Sparsity for Qubit Hamiltonians in Spherical Fermion Systems
abstract: For any $N$-fermion system whose single-particle orbitals are products of spherical harmonics and arbitrary radial functions, the fraction of nonzero two-body matrix elements is determined solely by angular momentum selection rules and is independent of the radial potential. Exact enumeration of the Gaunt coefficients yields the angular ERI density $D(l_{\max})$ under the Coulomb selection rule (conservation of total magnetic quantum number, $m_a+m_b=m_c+m_d$): $14.84%$ at $l_{\max}=1$, $8.52%$ at $l_{\max}=2$, $6.06%$ at $l_{\max}=3$, $4.83%$ at $l_{\max}=4$, and $3.99%$ at $l_{\max}=5$. At $l_{\max}=2$, $91.48%$ of all possible two-body matrix elements are guaranteed to vanish by the Wigner–Eckart theorem before any property of the potential is invoked. A stricter pair-diagonal restriction ($m_a=m_c$, $m_b=m_d$), applicable to axially-symmetric or $m$-decoupled bases, gives a further reduction ($2.76%$ at $l_{\max}=2$, $1.44%$ at $l_{\max}=3$). The bound is independent of the number of radial quantum numbers retained at fixed $l_{\max}$, and therefore independent of qubit count. Numerical verification across five potentials (Coulomb, harmonic oscillator, Woods–Saxon, square well, Yukawa) confirms the theorem: angular sparsity patterns are bit-identical across all potentials at matched orbital counts. The radial-angular factorization and the Gaunt selection rules are standard results from Condon & Shortley and Slater; the contribution of this paper is the explicit quantitative bound at each $l_{\max}$, framed as a universal resource guarantee for qubit Hamiltonian sparsity that applies to electronic structure, nuclear shell models, quantum dots, and any other spherical-potential fermion system.

title: The Bargmann–Segal Lattice: π-Free Discretization of the Harmonic Oscillator on S^5
abstract: We construct a discrete graph encoding of the three-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator on the holomorphic sector of $S^5$ and verify by exact rational arithmetic that the resulting graph and its projection to physical energies contain no transcendental constants. The Bargmann–Segal transform [ref] maps the harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian to $\hbar\omega(\hat{N} + 3/2)$ on the Fock–Bargmann space, where $\hat{N}$ is the Euler number operator on holomorphic monomials. Restricting to the unit sphere $S^5 \subset \mathbb{C}^3$ identifies the eigenspaces with the symmetric SU(3) irreps $(N, 0)$, of dimension $(N+1)(N+2)/2$, which match the harmonic oscillator shell degeneracies exactly. The graph constructed from these states with dipole transition weights computed by exact fractions.Fraction arithmetic is bit-exactly $π$-free at $N_{\max} = 5$ (56 nodes, 165 edges, zero irrationals encountered). The only $π$ in the construction is the Gaussian normalization $π^{-3}$ of the continuous Bargmann measure, which the discrete graph never invokes. The one-mode version of that measure is the large-spin limit of a spin's coherent-state measure on $S^2$, so the oscillator is also reached from the compact label set of a spin, with the $π$ entering only in the limit (Section (ref)). The Coulomb problem on $S^3$ and the harmonic oscillator on $S^5$ are both natural sphere quotients, but they live on different spheres with different geometric character (Riemannian vs complex), have natural operators of different order (second vs first), and yield spectra of different growth (quadratic vs linear). These differences do not decide where $π$ enters. In the Kustaanheimo–Stiefel frame the Coulomb problem is a four-dimensional oscillator cut by one constraint: its label set, its $n^2$ degeneracy and the Casimir $n^2 - 1$ sit exactly on the oscillator's integer lattice, the projection is linear at fixed energy (the charges of the Coulomb Sturmians, $Z = n p_0$), and the lift costs one fibre volume, $π/4$, which cancels in every ratio. The oscillator's spectral zeta values carry $π^2$ at even argument, as those of $S^3$ do. So $π$ enters both sides in the same two ways, through a measure and through spectral sums (Section (ref)), and what separates the two problems is representation theory and arithmetic.

title: The Universal/Coulomb Partition of the GeoVac Spectral Triple What belongs to angular momentum, what belongs to -Z/r, and why the difference matters
abstract: The GeoVac framework [ref] is a discrete spectral triple in the sense of Connes [ref] and the graph-spectral-triple lineage of Marcolli and van Suijlekom [ref]: an algebra $\mathcal{A}$ of functions on the Fock-projected discrete graph, a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of scalar and spinor states, and a Dirac operator $D$ inherited from the Camporesi–Higuchi spectrum on $S^3$. This paper identifies a clean structural decomposition of the framework's results into two disjoint sectors: • A universal sector, depending only on $\mathcal{A}$ and the angular structure of the basis. The angular sparsity theorem of Paper 22 [ref] — the angular ERI density is potential-independent (global-$M_L$ Coulomb $D=6.06%$ at $l_{\max}=3$, the density the composed pipeline realizes; the stricter pair-diagonal restriction gives $D_{\mathrm{pd}}=1.44%$), bit-identical across Coulomb, harmonic oscillator, Woods–Saxon, square well, and Yukawa potentials — is the canonical example. • A potential-specific sector, depending on the choice of $D$. The Fock projection rigidity theorem of Paper 23 [ref] ($S^3$ projection unique to $-Z/r$ by $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ symmetry) and the Bargmann–Segal rigidity theorem of Paper 24 [ref] (the 3D isotropic harmonic oscillator is the unique central potential whose spectrum arises from the Euler operator on $H^2(S^5)$ restricted to symmetric $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ irreps; its converse half rests on an imported result Paper 24 flags as unverified) jointly establish the partition's sharpness, the second subject to that caveat. The two rigidity theorems sit on opposite sides of an operator-order divide: Coulomb uses a second-order Riemannian Laplacian, the HO a first-order complex Euler operator. The divide does not decide where $π$ enters: both label sets are $π$-free, and on both sides $π$ enters through a measure and through spectral sums at even argument;\ in the Kustaanheimo–Stiefel frame the Coulomb problem is itself a constrained oscillator with a linear projection (Paper 24). The $S^5$ gauge-structure result of Paper 24 [ref] supplies the standing Coulomb/HO discriminator, Wilson gauge with natural matter coupling, decided by representation theory (on $S^3 = \mathrm{SU}(2)$ matter and links share a representation, on $S^5$ matter coupling needs a Clebsch–Gordan intertwiner). Calibration $π$, listed here as a second discriminator until 2026-10-19, is withdrawn. (A third, the spectrum-computing role of $L_0$, [retracted 2026-09-26: coulomb-ho-layer1-and-three-discriminators] was listed here until 2026-09-25; it is withdrawn, because the graph Laplacian on $S^3$ does not converge to the $S^3$ Laplacian and is spectrally inert there as on $S^5$.) We frame the partition in spectral-triple language and identify which features of GeoVac transfer to non-Coulomb systems for free, which require system-specific rederivation, and what this implies for nuclear, oscillator, and gauge-theoretic extensions of the framework.

title: Two-body interactions from the tensor-product spectral triple: Selection rules from the algebra, coupling strengths from the metric
abstract: We construct the tensor-product spectral triple $\mathcal{T}_{S^3} ⊗ \mathcal{T}_{S^3}$ for two particles on the Fock-projected three-sphere at finite cutoff $n_{\max}$, and investigate whether the gauged spectral action generates the Coulomb inter-particle interaction from the framework's own algebraic structure. The free tensor-product Dirac $D_{\mathrm{total}} = D_1 ⊗ I + \gamma_1 ⊗ D_2$ satisfies $\{D, \gamma\} = 0$ exactly, so $D_{\mathrm{total}}^2$ factorizes and the free spectral action contains no interaction (Theorem (ref)). Gauging via the inner fluctuation $A = \sum_i a_i^\dagger [D, a_i]$ from the truncated operator system $\mathcal{O}_{n_{\max}}$ produces a genuine two-body interaction: the connected (non-factorizable) fraction of $\{D, A\}$ is $77%$ at $n_{\max} = 2$ and $32%$ at $n_{\max} = 3$ (Proposition (ref)). This interaction is supported only on the direct (density–density) elements $\langle ab|\cdot|ab \rangle$, so it is $m$-conserving, $\Delta l = 0$ and pure $k = 0$ by construction (Theorem (ref)); the exchange and $k > 0$ channels of $1/r_{12}$ are absent. The radial matrix element ratios do not match the Coulomb $1/r_{12}$ kernel: the coefficient of variation exceeds $1600%$ and the Pearson correlation is $0.41$–$0.58$ (Proposition (ref)). These results precisely delineate Paper 31's universal/Coulomb partition at the two-body level: the gauged algebra yields a monopole, density–density subset of the Coulomb channels; the metric determines the coupling strengths. The multi-focal composition wall identified across six independent observables in the GeoVac programme is structurally located at this algebra/metric boundary.

title: Periods of GeoVac: a cyclotomic mixed-Tate census of the master Mellin engine
abstract: The GeoVac framework is a discrete spectral-graph approach to quantum mechanics built around the Fock conformal projection $ℝ^3 \hookrightarrow S³$. Its $S³$ spectral-zeta and heat-trace data (the census treated here; chemistry-side quadrature seeds, spectral determinants, and the elliptic period of Paper 61 lie outside it) empirically produce a constrained class of transcendental numbers:\ $π$ and integer powers thereof, classical odd zeta values $ζ(2k+1)$, Catalan $G = \beta(2)$ and the Dirichlet beta values $\beta(s) = L(s, \chi_{-4})$, and a depth-$k$ tower of constants at higher loop order, identified in closed form at $k = 2$ and $k = 3$ (Paper 28 of the GeoVac corpus). We prove that every such identified transcendental (the census above; the depth-$k$ tower beyond $k = 3$ is not yet identified) sits in cyclotomic mixed-Tate periods (localized at $π$) at level $\le 4$ over $\mathcal{O}_4[1/4] = \Z[i, 1/2]$, with a period-theoretic stratification, over the cases treated, read against the operator-order slot $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ of the master Mellin engine $\Mcal[\Tr(|D|^k e^{-tD^2})]$ on the discrete Camporesi–Higuchi $S³$ spectral triple: • $k = 0$ (volume slot, $\Vol(S^2)/4 = π$):\ $M_1 \subset \Q[π, π^{-1}]$, the localised pure-Tate algebra at $π$, depth $0$. • $k = 2$ (Seeley–DeWitt coefficients):\ $M_2 \subset \bigoplus_k π^{2k}\cdot\Q$, the pure-Tate even-weight sub-ring, strictly smaller than the generic Fathizadeh–Marcolli [ref] mixed-Tate classification of Robertson–Walker spectral actions: on the static $S³$ sub-case, the Dirac SD expansion is two-term exact and the scalar Laplacian SD coefficients form a closed geometric series. • $k = 1$ (vertex parity / Hurwitz at quarter-integer shifts / Dirichlet $L$):\ $M_3 \subset \MT(\Z[i, 1/2])$ at level $\le 4$ via Deligne [ref] and the explicit basis of Glanois [ref], at depth at most the loop order. The $\chi_{-4}$ parity split of the Dirac spectral sums is read as the Deligne–Glanois Galois descent from level $4$ to level $2$, at the level of motivic periods. The three sub-mechanisms are not set-theoretically disjoint (joint engagement is the typical case in physical observables); the master Mellin index $k$ indexes the period-ring contribution of each elementary spectral object (a reading, not a consequence of the conditional case-exhaustion theorem). We catalogue witnesses from across the corpus (Papers 2, 18, 28, 38, 40, 43, 50, 51) and indicate open questions: $S_{\min}$ is now fully resolved — both remaining Hoffman $t$-values are identified and $S_{\min} \in \Q[π^2, \ln 2, ζ(3), ζ(5)]$ in explicit closed form (Paper 28); inhomogeneous extension to non-static Robertson–Walker substrates; cross-manifold extension to the Bargmann–Segal Hardy lattice on $S⁵$; and inner-factor Yukawa coupling content.

title: The Tannakian substrate of GeoVac: a finite-cutoff pro-system, a neutral Tannakian category, and an explicit G_a^(3N) ⋊ SL_2 inclusion into Aut^(⊗)(ω)
abstract:
We construct the Tannakian substrate of the GeoVac spectral triple at finite cutoff and verify, bit-exact on explicit $sympy$-rational panels, every prerequisite of the Deligne–Milne 1982 neutral Tannakian theorem on an abelian primitive Hopf algebra $\HGV(n_max) = \Sym_{\Q}(V_{n_max})$ whose primitive space $V_{n_max}$ has $\Q$-dimension $3 N(n_max)$ (one generator per (sector, Mellin slot) pair). The construction has two halves. 
oindentPro-system half. A cofiltered system of finite-cutoff truncations $\{\HGV(n_max)\}_{n_max\in\N}$ with explicit Hopf-algebra transition maps $\Phi_{m, k} : \HGV(m) 	o \HGV(k)$ (block-diagonal truncations) satisfies the cofiltered axiom, is $\Ustar$-equivariant, admits a well-defined inverse limit $\Ginf \cong \Q^{\N_{\mathrm{sec}}}$ into which the continuum cochains $\chi_{\infty}$, $\eta_{\infty}$ and the continuum Mellin lift $F(s)$ of v3.66.0 FO1–FO3 project coherently, and has finite-cutoff endomorphism algebra $\End_{\mathrm{compat}}(\Oh_{n_max})$ that is block-lower-triangular of closed-form dimension $\dim = \sum_{j \le i \le n_max}(i + 1)(j + 1)$. 
oindentTannakian half. The finite-dimensional representation category $\Repcat(\HGV(n_max))$ is an abelian, symmetric monoidal, rigid $\Q$-linear category (axioms TC-1a, TC-1b, TC-1c bit-exact); the no-op forgetful $ω : \Repcat 	o \Vecbf_{\Q}$ is a faithful exact $⊗$-functor (TC-1d); and the candidate cosmic-Galois group $\Ulev = G_a^{3 N(n_max)} ⋊ SL_{2}$ admits an explicit inclusion \[ \Phimap : \Ulev(\Q) \longrightarrow Aut^{⊗}(ω), \qquad \Phimap(t, g)(V) = \exp\!\Bigl(\sum_{g\in\mathfrak{P}} t_{g} X_{g}^{V}\Bigr) ⊗ ho_{V_{\mathrm{PW}}}(g) \] on the natural-substrate panel $V ⊗ V_{\mathrm{PW}}$, which is bit-exact at every point of the verification grid (TC-1e + TC-1f). At $n_max = 2$ the inclusion is full-panel injective: for every one of the $3 \cdot N(2) = 15$ primitive generators $g$ a 2-dim test rep $V_{g}$ detects $g$ uniquely with $\eta_{V_{g}}(t) = I$ iff $t_{g} = 0$. \emph{Total bit-exact verification panel: $5{,}864$ zero residuals} ($sympy$-rational throughout) across PS-1/2/3/4 + TC-1a/b/c/d/e/f + TC-2a/b/c/d + G4-Inj at $n_max \in \{2, 3, 4\}$. The G4-Inj block ($2{,}904$ of these) holds by construction (multiplicativity of a ring map, a coproduct identity on the GeoVac side, the condition $\det g = 1$ on its $SL_{2}$ panel, and panel-size bookkeeping), so those residuals do not certify the comparison theorem (Theorem (ref)). The fourteenth math.OA standalone in the GeoVac series. 
oindentCosmic-Galois comparison homomorphism. Sending each M3 generator to the depth-1 de Rham class of its level-4 motivic period, and each M1 and M2 generator to $0$, gives a Hopf map out of the GeoVac Hopf algebra; dually it is a homomorphism from the unipotent radical $\mathcal{U}_{4}$ of the level-4 motivic Galois group $\mathcal{G}_{4} = \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{MT}(\Z[i, 1/2])}$ of Deligne 2010 + Glanois 2015 into the abelian factor $G_a^{3N}$ of GeoVac's group, factoring through $\mathcal{U}_{4}^{\mathrm{ab}}$, with image of dimension at most $2$ per weight (Section (ref), Theorem (ref)). The proof uses the Eskandari–Murty–Nemoto 2025 level-4 placement of $G$ + the Deligne 2010 faithful action (level 4) on $π_{1}^{\mathrm{mot}}(\Gm - \mu_{4})$. Depth-$\ge 2$ content, which a primitive Hopf substrate cannot receive, is the named long-range forward research question. 
oindentHonest scope. We close the inclusion direction $Aut^{⊗}(ω) \supseteq \Ulev$ at finite cutoff with both Levi factors explicit (TC-1e/TC-1f). The converse equality $Aut^{⊗}(ω) = \Ulev$ at finite cutoff is closed by the TC-2 sub-arc: TC-2a (abelian factor at $n_max = 2$), TC-2b ($SL_{2}$ factor on the Peter–Weyl panel), TC-2c (higher cutoffs $n_max \in \{3, 4\}$), and TC-2d (pro-system cofiltered coherence on the natural-substrate panel). The remaining long-range content is whether an enriched (non-primitive, depth $\ge 2$) GeoVac Hopf structure receives more of $\mathcal{U}_{4}$ than its abelianization — the pro-finite question coherent with v3.66.0 FO3 Interpretation C on $\Ginf$ (PS-3).

title: Forced and Free Content in the GeoVac Framework: An Observations Paper
abstract: The GeoVac framework produces a wide class of structural facts (the $(n,l,m)$ label set and its $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ Casimir spectrum, $\sphere{3}$ outer manifold, master Mellin engine, inner-algebra factor count, the $D_F$ moduli dimension $\dim \Mcal(\DF) = 32$ at one generation (matter-sector projection rank $16$; the factor count and this dimension hold relative to the Hopf-tower organizing reading, the adopted Upgrade B axiom and the imported CCM representation), the two-term spectral action on $\sphere{3}$ (Chamseddine–Connes), and many more), admits the gauge group $U(1) × SU(2) × SU(3)$ under an organizing reading plus an adopted axiom (Paper 32; not a derivation), and consumes specific numerical content as external input (Yukawa values, generation count, calibration cutoff moments, atomic-physics screening exponents, multi-loop QED counterterms, etc.). We catalogue both sides of this forced/free seam across the corpus — 43 forced entries (the gauge-group entries forced relative to the adopted Upgrade B axiom), 5 Observations ($\kappa$, matched not forced; the magnetic-moment ratio of Paper 28's vertex model, an unnormalized coincidence; two released-axis results that lack a derivation, the decompactification front and the four-body $r_{12}$ bridge; and the rung rule, a pattern across the tested instances), 1 admitted-not-forced entry, 27 calibration entries and 3 walls, spanning foundations, gauge structure, periods, gravity, QED, the Standard Model inner factor, multi-focal-composition walls, chemistry / quantum computing scaling, foundational calibration and the released axes of the chemistry program: a second nucleus, the decompactification front, a third and a fourth centre, bending, a three-electron chain, the four-body $r_{12}$ bridge, four linked densities and a ring of three densities, and, from the label set itself, a spin grown large, the hydrogen continuum, a finite nucleus and its magnetization, and the Kustaanheimo–Stiefel lift, each recorded with the number class that enters when the axis is released, where one is assigned — weight-one logarithms at two centres, an elliptic period at three, a K3 holomorphic period for the chain, a period not built from elliptic ones for four linked densities, and, at the fibre, an elliptic period again for a Coulomb ring of three, with dilogarithms at one centre; $π^{1/2}$ and $e^{-x^2}$, only as limits, for the spin; and one exponential of $π$ for the continuum; while a finite nucleus consumes moments of its charge as matching coefficients. We identify a cross-domain unity pattern (the same wall appears in seven settings, all carrying the same multi-focal-composition signature, the two nuclear ones sharing the textbook matching mechanism of nonrelativistic QED) and test five candidate principles for what discriminates the two sides: multi-focal depth, period-content classifiability, dimensional character, compactness inheritance, and packing-reachability. The fifth candidate (packing-reachability: an entry is forced iff a witness structural derivation exists from $\{$Paper 0 + standard real-spectral-triple axioms + Hopf-tower truncation + Bertrand + Upgrade B + CCM canonical SM representation$\}$) consolidates the forced/free boundary rather than independently discriminating it: its 98.3% agreement with the F/C status (59/60, on the 2026-06-08 labelling in which $\kappa$ and the anomalous-moment ratio were counted forced) is an internal-consistency check confirming the catalogue applies its conventions uniformly — the packing-reachable tag is the F/C label by construction — not an independent accuracy. The independent discriminator signal is carried by multi-focal depth, period class, and the two-family decomposition. The earlier-named two-family decomposition (multi-focal composition vs. inner-factor input data) is preserved as the structural failure-mode story beneath the principle: both families share the same surface verdict (packing-unreachability) but exhibit different structural reasons for it. This paper consolidates what was previously scattered across CLAUDE.md \S 1.7 working hypotheses, dead-end records, and individual sprint memos.

title: The Bessel-Moment Period Algebra of the Three-Center Coulomb Integral: Modular Structure and Cosmic-Galois Placement
abstract: The companion Paper 59 [ref] establishes that the radial core of the genuine three-center electron-repulsion integral over $1s$ Slater orbitals, read in momentum space under Fock's conformal projection, is a two-scale elliptic Bessel moment: a period of the rank-four irregular Picard–Fuchs connection of the genus-one curve $y^{2}=(c_{1}k^{2}+1)(c_{2}k^{2}+1)$; its finite closed form is open, and the integrated value, as a function of the bond angle, leaves the two-center class (Paper 59). This paper takes that object as its starting point and develops its number-theoretic structure. [MEASURED; classical] The elliptic family is the Legendre family over the modular curve $X(2)=\Gamma(2)\backslash\mathfrak{H}^{\ast}$, pulled back along the exact linear map $\lambda(\tau(\rho))=1-\rho$; the parameter integral sweeps the physical arc $\lambda<1$ of the real locus of $X(2)$ and passes through complex-multiplication fibres—at $\tau=i$ ($\rho=\tfrac12$, inside the physical domain) and $\tau=i\sqrt2$—where the periods are Chowla–Selberg $\Gamma$-values, so a molecular integral carries classical $\Gamma$-value periods across distinct fundamental discriminants. [OBSERVATION] The integrated observable lives on $X_{0}(2)$, is a $\Gamma(2)$ resurgent Lambert series (the pure multiple modular value being its regular $D\to0$ shadow), and its fibre carries conductor-$4$ ($\mathbb{Z}[i]$, $G=\beta(2)$) arithmetic through the theta series $K=\tfrac{π}{2}\theta_{3}^{2}$. That modular and complex-multiplication structure—not the integer-relation search—places the radial core inside the cosmic-Galois / mixed-elliptic-motive layer the program's Tannakian substrate reaches for; the guarded, decoy-calibrated searches are separately and decisively negative for a clean low-height closed form through weight three. [SYMBOLIC + MEASURED] The connection has four master periods whose Wronskian is the pure monomial $W_{0}D^{-2}$ and whose Lagrange bilinear concomitant—the analogue, here for the $\Gamma(2)$ (Legendre) family, of the Broadhurst–Roberts / Fresán–Sabbah–Yu quadratic period relations, whose proved case is the Kloosterman connection—is identified in closed form as $B=π \Omega$, with $\Omega$ the canonical integer symplectic intersection form, so the monodromy group lies in $\mathrm{Sp}_{4}(\mathbb{Z})$ (the differential Galois group, being a positive-dimensional algebraic group here, lies in $\mathrm{Sp}_{4}(\mathbb{C})$). The radial core is an Eisenstein / complex-multiplication Bessel-moment period, past the reach of the elliptic-dilogarithm mechanism; the integrated value is not a critical $L$-value of a $\Gamma(2)$ cusp form, and its class and explicit finite reduction remain the open frontier.

title: Linked Electron Densities Climb the Banana Ladder: Period Classes of Molecular Integrals over Exponential-Type Orbitals
abstract: Paper 59 read the radial core of the three-center electron-repulsion integral over $1s$ Slater orbitals as an elliptic Bessel moment: two two-center densities coupled by a Coulomb kernel build a genus-one curve. This paper asks two questions that result leaves open. How does the class climb when an integral links more densities? And how far does the reading reach past $1s$ orbitals? [SYMBOLIC PROOF + PRIOR ART] The second is answered first, in part, by a dictionary. Every exponential-type orbital on a center is a polynomial differential operator in its exponent and its center coordinate, with coefficients rational in the exponent, applied to the $1s$ Yukawa function on that center; at the fibre, for $s$-type densities, every density weight is a polynomial in $c$, $c^{-1}$ and the Euler operators $c \partial_c$ applied to the $1s$ weight. So every multi-density integral with rational kernels is that operator applied to the $1s$ integral of the same density graph and lies in that integral's $D$-module. For a tree of $s$-type densities on its one-scale slice the holomorphic period is a differential operator applied to the $1s$ one, so it sits at or below the $1s$ rung, and for $n\le8$, when it is not identically zero, on it. [MEASURED] In every case computed, all with $s$-type densities, a general-orbital integral sits on that rung. [SYMBOLIC + MEASURED] On the graph the rung is read off the holomorphic period. Any tree of $n$ linked two-center densities has the same period, a Bessel moment in $n$ scales;\ its one-scale family is annihilated by an operator of order $n$, which for $n=2$ to $5$ is the Hadamard product of the Legendre operator with the operator of the equal-mass banana integral with $n-1$ propagators: $n=2$ is Legendre's $K$, $n=3$ Clausen's elliptic square (a K3 surface), $n=4$ entry \#58 of the Calabi–Yau tables, the first period not built from elliptic ones, and $n=5$ brings no new type. The real three-dimensional star and path of four densities reduce onto that operator with no K3 piece. A fourth distinct center adds no genus [MEASURED]. [SYMBOLIC + MEASURED] A Coulomb ring of three densities does not climb: its loop integrates out by the three-dimensional uniqueness relation and it sits on the elliptic rung, below the chain of three; the correlated triangle of explicitly correlated methods, with exponential geminals on two edges, sits with the chain on the K3 rung at $\gamma=1$, $3/2$ and $2$, its geminal acting as an imaginary external momentum, and its operators follow from integration by parts on the kite and the tetrahedron. A Gaussian geminal leaves the ladder for exponential periods. [OBSERVATION] Read as a Feynman graph, every instance fits one pattern: the class is set by the shape of the density graph and the masses on its lines. We state it as a bounded conjecture. Trees sit at rung $n$; the rung names an operator and not a finite set of numbers, since on every slice tested the three-electron fibre is a K3 function integrated once and at generic scales it has no relation to the K3 and elliptic periods in any basis tried; rings are ordered by uniqueness, not by count; and the integrated value sits at or below its fibre. The caps are stated: the three-dimensional reduction is shown through four densities, the dictionary's rung bound only for $s$-type trees on the one-scale slice, the only ring tested is the triangle, and the generic fibre's content is evidence. [PRIOR ART] The operators are known in the mathematics of Bessel moments and banana integrals; the Averys' momentum-space treatment of these same integrals re-expands every two-center density in a one-center basis and reaches the genus-zero class only through an infinite, non-sparse series. What is new is the route from molecular integrals to the ladder, the dictionary that places every orbital's integral in the $D$-module of its graph's $1s$ integral, and the prospective records in which most rungs were registered before they were computed.

title: The Dimensionless Vacuum: Recovering the Schrödinger Equation on a Scale-Invariant Label Lattice
abstract: Fock showed in 1935 that stereographic projection turns the momentum-space hydrogen Schrödinger equation into a rotation-invariant integral equation on the unit three-sphere $S^3$, whose kernel $1/|\omega - \omega'|^2$ is zonal and diagonal on the hyperspherical harmonics (the eigenfunctions of the Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta_{S^3}$, eigenvalue $-(n^2-1)$). [PRIOR ART] On those harmonics the kernel acts as $2π^2(1-\Delta_{S^3})^{-1/2}$ (eigenvalue $2π^2/n$), so the bound-state Hamiltonian is a function of $\Delta_{S^3}$, $H = -\tfrac{Z^2}{2}(1-\Delta_{S^3})^{-1}$, i.e. $E_n = -Z^2/(2(C+1))$ with $C = n^2-1$ the $SO(4)$ Casimir: in this sense Fock's projection makes $\Delta_{S^3}$ equivalent to the Schrödinger problem. (The kernel is the restriction to $S^3$ of the Green's function of the $ℝ^4$ Laplacian, not the Green's function of $\Delta_{S^3}$.) [MEASURED] We report what the GeoVac discrete graph Laplacian is measured to do through $n_{\max} = 30$—[INTERNAL THEOREM] its top eigenvalue saturates the bipartite bound $\lambda_{\max} \to 2 d_{\max} = 8$ at the closed-form rate $(C_{\mathrm{sat}} + o(1))/n_{\max}^2$ (Paper 0 \S VI; $C_{\mathrm{sat}}$ a saturation constant, not the Casimir $C$), proved rather than sampled—but this saturation is the band edge of two-dimensional grid graphs (twice the maximum degree) and carries no $S^3$ information. [WALL] \gvc{graph-s3-wall}{The edge Laplacian $L = D - A$ does not converge to the $S^3$ Laplace–Beltrami operator: its edges never change $l$, so it splits into $n_{\max}$ disconnected $l$-blocks, and its kernel is $n_{\max}$-dimensional at every cutoff while $\Delta_{S^3}$ has a single zero mode (tests/test_graph_s3_nonconvergence.py)}. What survives is exact at every cutoff: the node set $(n, l, m)$, $n^2$ per shell, is the Gel'fand–Tsetlin label set of the Peter–Weyl truncation of $L^2(S^3)$, on which $-\Delta_{S^3} = \mathbf{L}^2 + \mathbf{A}^2$ acts as the diagonal $SO(4)$ Casimir $n^2 - 1$ (a node weight, not an edge Laplacian; standard $SO(4)$ representation theory). The $S^3$ equivalence itself is carried by Fock's continuum projection, whose chain we audit by symbolic computation (its non-definitional step, the kernel eigenvalue, is tested for $n \le 4$; general $n$ is Fock's). [PRIOR ART] The Laplace–Beltrami operator on the round unit $S^3$ has pure integer eigenvalues $\lambda_n = -(n^2 - 1)$ with no intrinsic physical scale (standard; checked symbolically for $n \le 4$). [SYMBOLIC PROOF] The Rydberg energy levels $E_n = -Z^2/(2n^2)$ enter only through the energy-shell constraint $p_0^2 = -2E$, which acts as a ``stereographic focal length'' mapping the unit sphere to flat $ℝ^3$ momentum coordinates; the quantization $p_0 = Z/n$ itself is forced by the eigenvalue $2π^2/n = \mathrm{Vol}(S^3)/n$ of Fock's $S^3$ Coulomb kernel on the degree-$(n-1)$ harmonics. [PRIOR ART] That eigenvalue holds for every $n$ (Fock 1935; the Funk–Hecke theorem); we verify it in exact arithmetic for $n \le 4$ and every $l < n$ (one real harmonic per $l$) without inputting $E_n$ (tests/test_paper7_fock_kernel.py). [SYMBOLIC PROOF + MEASURED] At positive energy the projection lands on the hyperboloid $H^3$: continuing $n \to iZ/k$ releases only the cap $l \le n-1$, and every continuum density tested is the continued bound one times the single factor $1/(1-e^{-2π Z/k})$, the ratio of the two normalizations (Section (ref), tests/test_paper7_hydrogen_continuum_door.py); the factor is standard quantum defect theory [ref]. At $E = 0$, the third shape, the Runge–Lenz algebra contracts to the Euclidean group and both sides meet one $π$-free threshold function. [SYMBOLIC PROOF] The projection geometry is audited by a suite of 18 symbolic checks (ten of them limiting-case, definitional or non-discriminating) covering the stereographic map, the conformal Laplacian and its $l = 0$ spectrum, and the (definitional) eigenvalue-to-energy bookkeeping.

title: Structurally Sparse Qubit Hamiltonians from Natural-Geometry Hydrogenic Bases
abstract: We show that qubit Hamiltonians built in natural-geometry hydrogenic bases, whose orbitals carry the $(n, l, m)$ labels of the GeoVac lattice, exhibit structurally favorable Pauli decompositions for quantum simulation. After Jordan–Wigner transformation, the GeoVac lattice Hamiltonian yields $\sim Q^{3.8}$ Pauli string terms in the number of qubits $Q$, compared to $O(Q^{4+})$ for conventional Gaussian-basis Hamiltonians (our own log-log fit of the published Pauli counts of Trenev et al. [ref] gives $Q^{4.25}$ for LiH and $Q^{3.92}$ for H$_2$O, spanning $Q^{3.9}$–$Q^{4.3}$). The advantage originates in angular momentum selection rules—enforced by Gaunt integrals at the two-electron integral level—which cause the electron repulsion integral (ERI) tensor density to decay as $\approx M^{\gvq{eri_decay_4pt}{-0.46}}$ with the number of spatial orbitals $M$ (four-point fit over $M = 5$–$55$; the $M = 5 \to 30$ endpoint slope is $M^{\gvq{eri_decay_2pt}{-0.49}}$), while Gaussian ERI tensors remain near-dense at $O(1)$. Beyond term counts, we quantify two operationally relevant cost metrics: the number of qubitwise-commuting (QWC) measurement groups scales as $O(Q^{4.05})$, and the Pauli 1-norm $\lambda = \sum_i |c_i|$—which controls both Trotter step counts and qubitization query complexity—scales as $O(Q^{1.78})$, $R^2 = 0.9997$. The 1-norm is strongly sub-quadratic and its equal-qubit advantage is $4.0×$ and $7.3×$—at matched qubit count, not matched accuracy, since the Gaussian bases give the lower He energy at both sizes; the QWC exponent, however, exceeds the Pauli term exponent and sits inside the Gaussian $O(Q^{4–5})$ band, so no measurement-group scaling advantage is claimed. The sub-quadratic 1-norm scaling is the key result for fault-tolerant simulation: it implies that Trotter circuit depth grows far more slowly with system size than term counts alone would suggest. The Gaussian baselines of the equal-qubit comparisons use computed integrals (Szabo and Ostlund for H$_2$; analytical STO and contracted cc-pVDZ/cc-pVTZ for He); the larger synthetic-integral Gaussian entries are illustrative only and carry no comparison. For composed multi-center systems, the pseudopotential approximation of the composed natural geometry framework [ref] yields block-diagonal electron repulsion integrals whose Pauli count factorizes exactly into a basis factor times the qubit count, $N_{\mathrm{Pauli}} = c(n_{\max}) Q$, with rational coefficients $c(1) = 3/2$, $c(2) = 279/10$, $c(3) = 7089/14$ identical across every molecule tested (eight systems, three periodic-table rows). Along the within-molecule basis axis the corresponding log–log exponent is $3.17$ (fit over $n_{\max} = 1$–$3$; molecule-independent to all reported digits), with the local slope rising toward $\sim 3.8$ by $n_{\max} = 4$—comparable to the atomic path and approaching the lower edge of the Gaussian span. The decisive advantage is therefore the system-size axis: at fixed basis the count is exactly linear in $Q$, against Gaussian baselines that scale as $Q^{3.9}$–$Q^{4.3}$ (published counts of Trenev et al. [ref], span fitted by us); at equal qubit counts this yields $51×$–$317×$ fewer Pauli terms for H$_2$O across $n_{\max} = 1$–$3$. These comparisons are at matched qubit counts, not matched accuracy; the composed basis carries classical equilibrium-geometry errors of 5.3–19.4% (LiH/BeH$_2$/H$_2$O; Sec. (ref)), making the framework optimal for fixed-geometry quantum simulation rather than geometry optimisation. Across the composed molecular library (35 molecules spanning $Z = 1$–56, H through Ba, including the first transition series ScH–ZnH), the composed Pauli count is exactly linear in the qubit count: $N_{\mathrm{Pauli}} = \gvq{composed_coeff}{27.90} × Q$ at $n_{\max} = 2$ (exact, non-identity terms; $d$-orbital blocks give 30.03). All counts in this paper are computed under the exact global-$M_L$ Coulomb selection rule ($m_a + m_b = m_c + m_d$). Until 2026-08-29 the production encoders realized a pair-diagonal restriction ($m_a=m_c$, $m_b=m_d$) that was documented as a deliberate sparsifying approximation but traced to a sign error in the Gaunt coefficient (the 3j magnetic argument $q = m_c - m_a$ instead of $m_a - m_c$); the corresponding retired coefficients were $11.10$ (main-group) and $9.23$ ($d$-block). Under the exact rule these become $\gvq{composed_coeff}{27.90}$ and $\gvq{composed_coeff_d}{30.03}$: the $d$-block coefficient is the larger of the two, so the $d$-block is denser than main-group and the apparent $d$-block sparsity advantage does not survive (Sec. (ref)).

title: The Periodic Table Recast as S_N Representation Theory on S^(3N-1)
abstract:
The non-relativistic $N$-electron Schrödinger equation, after separation of the hyperradius, reduces to angular dynamics on the hypersphere $S^{3N-1}$. The angular kinetic energy is the $\mathrm{SO}(3N)$ Casimir operator with eigenvalue $\mufree = 
u(
u + 3N - 2)/2$. Fermionic antisymmetry restricts the spatial wavefunction to a specific $S_N$ irreducible representation—the conjugate of the spin Young diagram $[n_\uparrow, n_\downarrow]$, a diagram with two columns of heights $n_\uparrow$ and $n_\downarrow$. The minimum angular quantum number compatible with it is the Pauli filling count $
u_{\min} = E(n_\uparrow) + E(n_\downarrow)$, where $E(m)$ sums the $m$ lowest one-particle polynomial degrees and degree $d$ holds $(d+1)(d+2)/2$ polynomials. We prove this for all $N$ and $S$ from Schur–Weyl duality (the minimal-quanta statement for non-interacting particles in an oscillator is prior art, Theorem 1 of Rittenhouse et al., whose proof they credit to Cavagnero (1986); it holds for any non-interacting $N$ (it is applied there to balanced spin populations); what is new here is the $S_N$/Schur–Weyl proof route and the atomic tabulation) and corroborate it by an exact character count for all spins through $N = 12$ and by brute force for $N = 3, 4$. It depends on the spin, equals $N-2$ exactly when both columns lie in the first two oscillator shells ($1 \le n_\downarrow \le n_\uparrow \le 4$; at lowest spin, for $2 \le N \le 8$), and grows as $N^{4/3}$; the ground-state orbital angular momentum and parity can raise it further (lithium's ${}^2S$ needs $
u = 2$, not 1). The $S_N$ irrep depends only on $N$ and $S$, so it cannot by itself separate the chemical groups (noble gases and alkaline earths share an irrep, and every doublet shares the alkali shape); together with the shell occupancy, an empirical configuration input, it yields a classification of atoms into five types—A (trivial), B (noble gas), C (alkali), D (alkaline earth), E (open shell)—that recasts the periodic table's group structure in representation-theoretic language. The periodic law corresponds to the repetition of the type sequence $\mathrm{C} 	o \mathrm{D} 	o \mathrm{E} 	o \mathrm{B}$ within each period. This classification maps onto, rather than predicts, the known periodic table structure; its value lies in providing a unified group-theoretic framework for a pattern that is usually described empirically. The angular quantities ($
u$, $\mufree$) are integers defined for every $N$, with nothing special at $Z = 1/α \approx 137$; we read the Dirac instability as a metric rather than a topological effect (an interpretive observation, not derived here).

title: Structurally Sparse Molecular Hamiltonians for Near-Term Quantum Simulation
abstract: We present a library of qubit Hamiltonians for molecular quantum simulation that are structurally sparser than conventional Gaussian-basis alternatives across a range that depends strongly on the comparison: from $0.28×$ (H$_2$O against minimal-basis STO-3G, i.e. denser) through $55$–$76×$ against cc-pVDZ, to $317×$ at the most favourable equal-qubit point. None of these is a matched-accuracy comparison. The Hamiltonians are constructed from a spectral graph theory framework (GeoVac) that exploits natural coordinate separations in molecular electronic structure, producing block-diagonal electron repulsion integrals and Gaunt-enforced selection rules that persist through Jordan-Wigner encoding. For the composed architecture (PK-partitioned), the composed LiH Hamiltonian has $1.33×$ more Pauli terms than raw minimal-basis STO-3G (\gvq{lih_composed_pauli}{838} vs. \gvq{lih_sto3g_raw}{631}; $3.0×$ more than the 276 reduced) and about twice its 1-norm, with $2.8×$ fewer qubit-wise-commuting measurement groups, while using more qubits; the decisive resource advantages are the exact linearity of the Pauli count in $Q$ across molecules at fixed basis and a 76$×$ reduction versus cc-pVDZ (all counts under the exact global-$M_L$ ERI rule, Sec. (ref)). The balanced coupled architecture (PK-free) gives a LiH FCI potential-energy-surface (PES) minimum at a computed $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 3.227$ bohr (7.0% above the experimental 3.015 bohr) at $n_{\max}=2$ (\gvq{lih_balanced_pauli}{2{,}726} Pauli terms, 30 qubits); a single-point evaluation at the experimental geometry reaches 0.20% energy error at $n_{\max}=3$ (84 qubits) when solved exactly. Chemistry-accuracy scope at $n_{\max}=2$ is row-conditional: LiH, the one first-row hydride with a computed PES, has an interior minimum, while second-row hydrides (NaH and below) exhibit monotone overattraction under every tested configuration — frozen-core balanced, multi-zeta valence, screened cross-center, explicit-core Hartree–Fock — with no interior PES minimum at the qubit-Hamiltonian level. We document this scope boundary empirically in \S(ref); the framework's primary value proposition is structural sparsity with quantitative truncation-convergence bounds (Paper 38 state-space GH convergence of the truncated $S^3$ triple, not of the molecular Hamiltonians), not energy-accuracy parity with CCSD(T) on second-row systems. The hamiltonian() registry covers 37 systems (35 composed molecules spanning $Z=1$–56, H through Ba, plus the He and H$_2$ reference atoms), including multi-center systems (CO, N$_2$, F$_2$), mixed frozen-core molecules (NaCl), and the full first transition series as hydrides (ScH through ZnH), with the within-molecule basis exponent $3.17$ identical across all three rows (small-basis fit, $n_{\max} \le 3$; local slope rising toward $\sim 3.8$)—and, on the two-point $n_{\max}=1,2$ fit, an exponent of $2.8163$ identical across all six molecules to the digits shown, forced by the exact $Q$-linearity at each basis rather than fitted—compared to $O(Q^{3.9–4.3})$ for Gaussian baselines. The composed Pauli count is exactly linear in qubit count (coefficient $\gvq{composed_coeff}{27.90}$, exact, for main-group molecules; $30.03$ for $d$-orbital blocks — both under the exact global-$M_L$ ERI rule, Sec. (ref)), so adding atoms to a molecule increases quantum cost linearly. Second- and third-row molecules use analytical frozen cores ([Ne], [Ar], [Ar]3$d^{10}$); the frozen-core energy enters only through the identity operator and does not affect quantum measurement cost. Isostructural molecules with frozen cores produce identical Pauli counts across periodic table rows. The Hamiltonians are available as a Python library with Qiskit, OpenFermion, and PennyLane export.

title: Nuclear Shell Model Hamiltonians on the Hyperspherical Lattice
abstract: We present structurally sparse qubit Hamiltonians for the nuclear shell model, constructed by applying the GeoVac angular-sparsity framework to the harmonic oscillator (HO) single-particle basis with a Mayer–Jensen spin–orbit term. The HO shell closures $2, 8, 20, 40, 70, 112$ follow from state counting on the oscillator labels, and the physical magic numbers $2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126$ are recovered with a spin–orbit strength $v_{ls}/\hbar\omega \approx 0.17$ and a Nilsson $\ell(\ell+1)$ correction $d_{\ell\ell}/\hbar\omega \approx 0.02$. We build a two-species qubit encoding for the deuteron ($1p+1n$, $16$ qubits, \gvq{p23_deuteron_pauli}{688} non-identity Pauli terms, $1$-norm $\approx 384$ MeV) using the Minnesota nucleon–nucleon potential and Moshinsky–Talmi brackets, and extend the architecture to helium-4 ($2p+2n$, $16$ qubits, \gvq{p23_he4_pauli}{904} Pauli terms) with intra-species antisymmetrization and proton–proton Coulomb repulsion;\ each encoded Hamiltonian reproduces its full-CI spectrum in the physical particle-number sector to $2× 10^{-12}$ MeV. He-4 has \gvq{p23_he4_deuteron_pauli_ratio}{1.31}$×$ the deuteron's Pauli terms, the added proton–proton and neutron–neutron channels; its $12.25×$ larger Hilbert space costs no terms, because at fixed qubit count the Jordan–Wigner term set does not depend on the particle number. A composed nuclear–electronic encoding ($26$ qubits), a deuteron nuclear block coupled to a hydrogen-like electron through a proton-spin hyperfine term, exercises the multi-block architecture and quantifies the $\sim 10^{13}$ coefficient ratio between nuclear, electronic, and hyperfine scales. We state and apply the Fock projection rigidity theorem: the $S^3$ conformal projection that makes the one-electron Coulomb Hamiltonian equivalent to the $S^3$ Laplace–Beltrami operator (whose harmonics the GeoVac lattice's nodes label) requires the hydrogenic spectrum, and does not extend to HO or Woods–Saxon systems. A finite nucleus breaks it in a controlled way: the labels survive, $n$ is released from being a whole number, and the $s$-wave quantum defect $-(2/5)(ZR)^2$ is the same for every $n$ and continues across threshold, moments of the nuclear charge being consumed as the matching coefficients of an effective theory; a finite magnetization is priced the same way, the Zemach moment first, with a logarithm set by the charge alone; in the Dirac equation near and past $Zα = 1$ the radius becomes compulsory (Sec. (ref)). For nuclear Hamiltonians, the GeoVac contribution is therefore the angular machinery and qubit encoding, not the conformal projection. All nuclear physics inputs (Minnesota strengths and ranges, used without the potential's space-exchange mixture; spin–orbit strength, $\hbar\omega$) follow the standard shell-model literature; the quantitative binding energies at $N_{\mathrm{shells}}=2$ are far from experiment and should be read as encoding-validation benchmarks, not as a nuclear-structure calculation.

title: Periods of Dirac Spectral Sums on S^3
abstract: We determine the periods of spectral sums built from the Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac spectrum on the unit three-sphere, $|\lambda_n| = n + 3/2$ with degeneracy $2(n+1)(n+2)$. (1) T9: the spectral zeta function of $D^2$ is a two-term polynomial in $π^2$ with rational coefficients at every integer $s \ge 1$; at half-integer $s \ge 5/2$ the same closed form carries odd zeta values (Theorem (ref)). (2) Parity: the Dirac Dirichlet series $D(s)$ lies in $\mathbb{Q}[π^2]$ at even $s$ and is a rational combination of $ζ(s{-}2)$ and $ζ(s)$ at odd $s \ge 5$ (Theorem (ref)). (3) \textbf{The $\chi_{-4}$ split:} the sub-sums over even and odd $n$ satisfy $D_{\mathrm{even}}(s) - D_{\mathrm{odd}}(s) = 2^{s-1}(\beta(s) - \beta(s{-}2))$ at every integer $s \ge 2$, so Catalan's $G$ and $\beta(4)$ appear in each half at $s = 4$ and cancel in the sum (Theorem (ref)). (4) Multi-loop chain sums: the two-loop sum is $2S_{\min}$, with $S_{\min}$ in closed form in $\mathbb{Q}[π^2, \ln 2, ζ(3), ζ(5)]$ (Hoffman double $t$-values, each reducing to depth $\le 1$); the three-loop sum $S^{(3)} = 40.6554\ldots$ (rigorous bracket $[40.65339, 40.65578]$) has an explicit closed form in $\mathbb{Q}[π^2, \ln 2, ζ(3), ζ(5), ζ(5,3)]$, in which $ζ(5,3)$, at coefficient $6π^2$, is the only constant beyond single zeta values and every level-2 depth-2 generator cancels; the four-loop sum has realized depth $\le 3$. Realized depth is $\le k-1$ at loop order $k = 2, 3, 4$ (Proposition (ref)). (5) Sommerfeld sums: the degeneracy-weighted coefficient sums $D_p$ of the exact Dirac hydrogen spectrum are weight-$(2p{-}1)$ zeta polynomials in which $ζ(2)ζ(2p{-}3)$ cancels and $\max(0, \lfloor(2p{-}5)/2\rfloor)$ products survive, observed through $p = 6$ (Observations (ref), (ref)); a shell-sum identity removes $ζ(s{-}1)$ from a fine-structure Dirichlet series (Theorem (ref)). The multi-loop sums are defined sums: their vertex weights come from a vertex model, the scalar-harmonic triangle with a parity clause (Eq. (ref)). The physical vector-photon vertex on $S^3$ obeys a different rule (Paper 33), so the period statements are statements about the sums as defined. Two results whose reading depends on the vertex rule are stated for the model: the ground-state zero of the model's one-loop self-energy (Theorem (ref)), which fails for the physical vertex, and an unnormalized one-loop magnetic-moment ratio (Sec. (ref)), whose normalization is owed.

title: The Fine Structure Constant as a Spectral Coincidence on the Three-Sphere
abstract: We record a numerical observation. The number $K = π(42 + π^2/6 - 1/40) = 137.036064$ lies within $4.8×10^{-7}$ (relative) of the inverse fine structure constant $α^{-1}$, and the smallest positive root of the cubic $α^3 - Kα + 1 = 0$ lies within $8.8×10^{-8}$ of $α$ (CODATA 2018). The three ingredients are spectral data of the unit three-sphere $S^3$: $B = 42$ is the degeneracy-weighted trace of the $SO(3)$ Casimir $l(l+1)$ over the scalar $S^3$ harmonics of the first three shells, the cutoff being the only one at which $B/N = \dim S^3 = 3$; $F = ζ(2) = π^2/6$ is the Dirichlet series of the shell degeneracy $n^2$ at $s = 4$; and $\Delta = 1/40$ is the reciprocal of a Dirac degeneracy on $S^3$. The combination rule $K = π(B + F - \Delta)$ is an Observation, not a derivation: its weights, signs, prefactor and the cubic are chosen, and we list which steps are computed and which are chosen. In a search over $N = 1.92×10^9$ formulas built from ingredients of the same kind, ten match $α$ more closely ($p = 5.2×10^{-9}$ per formula), so the expected chance count is $Np \approx 10$: within that search the formula is not unusual. The search was run after the formula was found and does not correct for that. Twelve mechanisms proposed to generate all three ingredients from one spectral construction were tested and eliminated; we tabulate them.

title: Wilson Lattice Gauge Theory on the GeoVac Label Graphs: Exact Factorization on the Scalar Graph and Compact U(1) on the Dirac Rule-B Graph
abstract: The GeoVac label graphs carry Wilson lattice gauge theories, and the two graphs studied here sit at opposite ends of solvability. On the scalar label graph, whose vertices are the labels $(n,l,m)$ of the $S^3$ harmonics, no edge changes $l$, and each $l$-block is a planar $(n_{\max}-l)×(2l+1)$ grid. Taking the plaquettes to be the graph's 4-cycles (the unit squares of these grids), the plaquettes form a basis of the cycle space at every $n_{\max}$, so after gauge fixing on a spanning tree the plaquette holonomies are independent Haar variables. $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ Wilson theory on this graph is therefore the exactly solvable two-dimensional lattice gauge theory: $Z(\beta) = [2e^{-\beta} I_1(\beta)/\beta]^{\beta_1}$, and every closed loop enclosing $A$ plaquettes has $\langle W \rangle = (I_2(\beta)/I_1(\beta))^{A}$, an area law by factorization that carries no information about confinement. The weak-coupling expansion gives the curl form $(\beta/8)\sum_a \langle A^a, B_2 B_2^{\top} A^a\rangle$, which is supported on the cycle space and completes the edge Laplacian $B^{\top}B$ to the full Hodge-1 Laplacian of the plaquette-filled complex; the cubic term is nonzero, with a vertex proportional to $\epsilon^{abc}$. Restricting the links to the maximal torus gives compact $U(1)$ Wilson theory, with $\langle W\rangle = (I_1/I_0)^A$, and we record the abelian dictionary between Wilson and graph-Hodge data together with the exact $n_{\max}=3$ edge-Laplacian spectrum. On the Dirac Rule-B graph, whose edges are E1 dipole transitions and all change $l$, the graph is connected, its 4-cycles outnumber the independent cycles ($44$ against $11$ at $n_{\max}=2$) and close into 2-cycles of three plaquettes, so compact $U(1)$ does not factorize. Seven standard diagnostics are compatible with compact $U(1)$ and discriminate no dimension: the monopole density falls roughly exponentially in $\beta$ on a range below the four-dimensional transition, full Monte Carlo Wilson loops resolve no area law (the area coefficient of a joint area-plus-perimeter fit is consistent with zero at $n_{\max}=2$), and the Polyakov loop on the product graph with a time circle is well defined through one extra cohomology class, while its expectation vanishes by centre symmetry. Each Rule-B link lies in many plaquettes ($8.8$ and $37.5$ on average at $n_{\max}=2,3$), so the comparison class is mean-field or large-dimension lattice gauge theory, not a three-dimensional lattice. The label graphs have no continuum limit, and nothing here bears on one.

title: Selection Rules of the Vector-Photon Vertex on S^3: the Physical Vertex, the Vertex Model and the Graph
abstract: We compute the electron–photon vertex $V = \int_{S^3} \langle \psi_1, c(A) \psi_2 \rangle$ on the round unit three-sphere, with $\psi_{1,2}$ Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac eigenspinors, $A$ a coclosed 1-form eigenform and $c$ Clifford multiplication, and use it to score eight selection rules. Representation theory of $\mathrm{Spin}(4) = \mathrm{SU}(2)_L × \mathrm{SU}(2)_R$ gives the rule, and two independent exact computations confirm it with no extra channel and no accidental zero: a group-theoretic route through Clebsch–Gordan coefficients (896 cells: sign pair, photon component and levels $n_1, n_2 \le 3$, $q \le 7$) and a coordinate route by exact monomial integration in $ℝ^4$ (360 cells), which agree wherever both run. For spinors of the same sign of $D$ the vertex keeps the window $|n_1 - n_2| < q < n_1 + n_2$, $n_1 + n_2 + q$ odd, of the vertex model used for spectral sums in Paper 28, and adds the channel $q = n_1 + n_2 + 1$. For opposite signs it opens channels with $n_1 + n_2 + q$ even, which the model has none of. The ground state couples, also to itself: the diagonal vertex $V(a, a)$ does not vanish. The Ward–Takahashi identity $\langle u, c(df) v \rangle = (\lambda_u - \lambda_v)\langle u, f v\rangle$ holds exactly. Each of the eight rules is scored three ways: on the GeoVac graph (scalar Fock graph 1/8, native Dirac graph 4/8, the latter by the definition of its edges), in the vertex model, and with the physical vertex. With the physical vertex, rules 1 (triangle sparsity) and 4 ($\Delta m$) hold, rule 6 holds in Ward–Takahashi form, and rules 2 (ground-state zero), 5 (E1 parity) and 8 ($q \le n_1 + n_2$) fail; rule 3 holds as a statement of representation theory but not as the model's channel-count table; for rule 7 the diagonal-vertex zero fails and Furry's theorem itself is not decided without charge conjugation and three-vertex traces. The $1{+}6{+}1$ partition that the vertex model gives does not survive the physical vertex. Kept from the graph and model analyses: the pendant-edge value $\Sigma_{\mathrm{graph}}(\mathrm{GS}) = 2(n_{\max}-1)/n_{\max}$, the fact that the edge Laplacian does not block-diagonalize by photon labels $(q, m_q)$, the diagonal $α_z$ identity of the model, and the normalization identity $\Sigma_{l=1} = 1/(4π)$. Coupling normalization, regularization and the gauge sector are owed.

title: A Convergent Discrete Replica Derivative on the Spinor Cone, with the Two-Term Camporesi–Higuchi Spectral Action on S^3 × S^1
abstract: We prove one new theorem and record the two continuum results it serves. The theorem concerns a finite-difference discretization of the two-dimensional cone of apex angle $2πα$ carrying an anti-periodic (spinor) field: its heat trace $K_n(α, t)$ converges to the continuum heat trace in $C^1$ in $α$ near $α = 1$, so the replica derivative $dK_n/dα|_{α=1}$, whose mode sum carries an extra weight $(j+\tfrac12)$, converges, and that weight costs nothing in the rate (Theorem (ref)). The proof dominates the mode series and its $α$-derivative by one summable Gaussian sequence. Numerically, the replica combination converges to the continuum value $1/6$, at order $O(a)$ in the radial spacing $a$ on the production grid. The continuum results are these. (i) The Chamseddine–Connes spectral action of the Camporesi–Higuchi Dirac operator on $S³_R$ and on $S³_R × S^1_\beta$ has exactly two power-law terms, up to exponentially small corrections. This is Chamseddine and Connes's result (by Poisson summation); we give an alternative proof through the Bernoulli identity $B_{2k+1}(3/2) = (2k{+}1)/4^k$, which makes the spectral zeta function vanish at every non-positive integer. The scalar and transverse-traceless tensor heat traces on $S³$ do not truncate. (ii) Traced over the rank-4 spinor bundle, the action's Einstein–Hilbert coefficient gives $G = 3π/(\phi(1)\Lambda^2)$ for a cutoff with Mellin moments $\phi(s)$. The replica derivative of the black-hole cigar's tip term, with the Dirac cone coefficient $-(1/12)(1/α - α)$ and the fermionic sign of the effective action, gives $S_{\BH} = A\Lambda^2\phi(1)/(12π) = A/(4G)$, positive and with the same $G$. That the two routes agree is the induced-gravity statement of Susskind–Uglum and Frolov–Fursaev, specialised to this spectrum. The absence of higher-curvature terms holds on the conformally flat $S³ × S^1$; the cigar is not conformally flat, and there the two routes agree at leading order in $\Lambda$. We also show that the second variation of the action on the $(1,1)$ sector of $SO(4)$ cannot distinguish the diagonal-$SU(2)$ spins $J = 0, 1, 2$, so it cannot by itself isolate a graviton. None of these results uses the GeoVac label lattice: they concern the continuum Camporesi–Higuchi spectrum and a finite-difference cone.

title: Entanglement Structure of the Angular Momentum Eigenbasis: Correlation in the Electron Repulsion and Basis-Intrinsic Sparsity
abstract: We characterize the entanglement structure of multi-electron atoms in the angular momentum eigenbasis—the basis whose orbitals are products of hydrogenic radial functions and spherical harmonics, labeled by quantum numbers $(n, l, m)$. Four computational results are presented. First, the location of correlation: at the fixed exponent $k=Z$ the one-body Hamiltonian of a He-like ion is exactly diagonal in this basis, so the off-diagonal electron repulsion carries all of the correlation energy and all of the entanglement, and the entanglement entropy scales as $S \sim Z^{-2.52}$ across He-like ions. (An earlier version assigned $10$–$39%$ of the correlation energy to a ``graph Laplacian'' [retracted 2026-09-25: he-graph-native-hop-headline] off-diagonal one-body term; that term is not part of the ion's Hamiltonian and the attribution is withdrawn, Sec. (ref). Added to the Hamiltonian as a model perturbation it does illustrate the one-body entanglement-inertness theorem of Paper 27: it moves the model energy by $10$–$39%$ of the correlation energy while its layer-attributed [retracted 2026-09-25: he-graph-native-hop-headline] share of the entanglement is $<0.2%$, although adding it changes $S$ at $Z=2$ by $7%$.) Second, basis-intrinsic sparsity: for systems with spherical symmetry, the angular momentum eigenbasis gives sparse electron repulsion integrals (ERIs), and a generic unitary rotation of the orbital indices, no matter how small, fills the ERI tensor from $17%$ to $100%$ density in a rapid but graded transition at the identity. The sparse bases are not isolated: a common rotation of the coordinate frame mixes the $m$ labels and leaves every ERI unchanged. The nonzero ERI count is $Z$-independent, confirming that sparsity is purely geometric. Third, entanglement network topology: orbital mutual information maps reveal a hub migration pattern—$1s \to 2s \to 2p$—that tracks the partially filled shell across the first row of the periodic table (for $Z = 5$–$9$ the ground states are degenerate multiplets and the hub shares depend on the member; for $Z = 7$–$9$, where members were sampled, the values and even the presence of a nonzero valence network do too).
